Value computer feedback for responding to every student regardless of who they are, being less threatening and more programmed — which matters because teachers' claimed flexibility about when and to whom to give feedback leaves many students without any.

Aim to increase the number of active learners rather than matching teaching to learner passivity: passive learners prefer organized, structurally clear, objective-specific teachers, while active learners prefer interaction, varied approaches and high enthusiasm.
Recognise highly structured direct teaching that emphasises testing and feedback as the most effective teaching form in school-effectiveness reviews.

Use student ratings of teaching, which relate to learning outcomes and are reliable, trustworthy and valid despite the popularity-contest dismissal, while noting the feedback they give teachers rarely translates into improvement on its own.
Make repeated testing effective by routing results to teachers who then modify instruction to address the strengths and gaps revealed; without that loop it is not feedback.

Keep the out-of-school baseline in view: students spend roughly 15,000 hours in school against some 29,000 hours at home over the same years and 26,000 hours with caregivers beforehand, so what the child brings from outside school is critical.
Treat gender differences in achievement as close to trivial (d = 0.12 across 41 meta-analyses and over five million people) and refuse gender-differentiated teaching justified by them.
Target attitude to the subject rather than generalized personality: it affects achievement as much and is far more amenable to teacher influence, with no major differences by sex or grade.

Apply the gender similarity hypothesis: across 124 meta-analyses males and females are alike on most psychological variables, verbal ability differences are virtually zero, and there is more variance within each gender than between them.
Note self-regulation as the clearest gender exception — girls score much higher on effortful control (d = 1.01) and inhibitory control (0.41) — without generalizing it to achievement.
Guard against adults' beliefs about sex differences causing mathematically talented girls and reading-talented boys to be overlooked.
Treat multi-grade and multi-age classes as neither better nor worse than single-grade (achievement d = 0.00 to -0.03) with small positive effects on attitude, self-concept and personal adjustment.

Reject single-sex classes as an achievement intervention: a study randomizing students and teachers found no gains for girls or boys in single-sex mathematics classes, and brighter students benefited more from mixed-sex classes.

Treat single-sex versus coeducational comparisons as confounded: single-sex classes tend to be selective in both students and teachers, so any difference may reflect selection rather than composition, and teaching quality and expectations produce far more powerful effects either way.
Reject ethnic matching of teacher to student as an achievement intervention: it makes essentially no difference (d = 0.02 reading, 0.03 mathematics).
Do not justify character and values education on academic grounds: it moves behaviour and attitude only modestly (d = 0.24) and achievement less (0.20).
Reject individualized instruction as a lever (d = 0.23, rank 100 of 138), and note it contributes little to self-esteem, critical thinking or attitude to the subject either.
Screen at entry on preschool mathematics and early reading only: externalizing and internalizing problem behaviours and social skills did not correlate with later academic success.
Use attention distractibility, internalizing behaviour problems, language variables and general cognitive functioning as the best early predictors of later achievement.

Ask parents to teach specific literacy skills (d = 1.15) rather than listen to the child read (0.51) or read to the child (0.18); the pattern held from kindergarten to grade 3, for children with and without reading difficulties, and across socioeconomic groups.
Locate desegregation achievement effects where they actually appear — the earliest primary grades, in reading rather than mathematics, and only in studies running more than one year.

Take early divergence seriously: ability at 22 months predicted achievement at 26, bottom- quartile infants were significantly less likely to gain any qualifications, and social-class effects were already marked at 22 months with variability increasing over time.
Challenge the at-risk and drop-out labels as socially constructed: they differentiate students only on IQ, educational aspirations and locus of control, and vary by region.

Read low self-esteem and negative coping in struggling adolescents largely as consequences of earlier lack of academic success, and treat diagnostic labels applied at that stage as over-used explanations even though they name real phenomena.

Do not let a disability label set the instructional expectation: around three-quarters of students labelled learning disabled exceeded the average student with emotional and behavioural disabilities, and labelled students often showed no difference on many school-related behaviours.

Treat the learning-difficulties label as itself depressing performance: 73 per cent of unlabeled low achievers scored above the average labeled low achiever (d = 0.61), with no evidence the labeled students differ qualitatively in learner characteristics.

Take seriously that students with learning disabilities are assessed as having social skill deficits by every rater — teachers, peers and themselves, with self-assessments harsher — and that their perception of their classroom status is accurate.

Diagnose learning disability as a circumscribed processing difficulty after evaluating instruction, opportunity, sensory and emotional factors, language, culture, disadvantage, and co-occurring conditions.
Treat adult learning-disability prevalence, continuity, and outcomes as uncertain and heterogeneous; group risks do not determine an individual's future.

Question the volume of testing given that students already hold much of the information it supplies — high school students estimate their own achievement at r above 0.80 — while warning that self-expectations set below attainable levels become a performance ceiling.

Reject the claim that making students feel good about themselves will make achievement follow: the relationship between self-measures and achievement is low though positive at about r = 0.20, replicated across the United States and Europe.
Expect conceptual-change effects to be large overall (d = 0.80) and largest on domain knowledge (1.31), then topic beliefs (0.89), concept knowledge (0.69) and topic knowledge (0.63).

Separate personality from self-belief: anxiety, dogmatism, extraversion, locus of control and neuroticism relate to achievement at close to zero, whereas self-efficacy, self-concept, motivation and persistence are among the larger correlates.

Target self-efficacy specifically: it has among the strongest relationships to achievement of all self-measures, and confidence is both a powerful precursor and a powerful outcome, especially in the face of adversity or error.
Do not conflate student traits with student beliefs: personality contributes almost nothing (0.06 to 0.10) while self-concept (0.32 to 0.41) and self-efficacy (0.37 to 0.76) contribute materially.
Of the Big Five treat only conscientiousness as appreciably related to achievement (d = 0.44), with neuroticism, extraversion, openness and agreeableness at or near zero.
Distinguish what a student can do (cognitive ability) from what a student will do (personality traits), and expect the two to combine into a better predictor as students get older.
Model self-concept as a rope of many overlapping fibres rather than one dominant self-view, and expect it to operate through how a person selects and interprets information.
Adopt the reciprocal-effects model of self-concept and achievement, which has the most support, rather than assuming either direction of causation alone.

Work on self-strategies rather than self-concept level: achievement rises when students invoke learning rather than performance strategies, accept rather than discount feedback, benchmark against difficult goals, compare themselves to subject criteria rather than to other students, hold high efficacy for learning, and self-regulate rather than fall into learned helplessness.
Reframe motivation away from push or pull, which presumes a static learner: students are already choosing constantly, so the question is why they invest in this task rather than that one.

Recognise the minimax principle — minimal effort for maximum gain — as strategically rational for a student though it does not enhance learning, and expect blanket demands for more effort to be resisted.

Use challenging learning intentions to induce greater effort and more of the student's total capacity than low-demand conditions do, since the rate of learning is a direct function of goal difficulty.

Establish that students believe their effort can make a difference, since no student has reason to invest in study unless they hold that belief and internal control is associated with higher achievement.
Require active teacher involvement in homework, since homework without it does not contribute to student learning, just as technologies show no major effect without teacher involvement.
Refuse visible busyness as evidence of learning: students who look engaged and appear to be putting in effort are not necessarily achieving, and busy work alone makes no difference.
Focus lesson activities on the learning intention rather than on busy work students may enjoy but which bears little relation to what is to be learnt.

Do not expect engagement and concentration effects to differ by ethnicity: no differences were found between African American and white students in need for achievement, personal expectations, hopelessness, denial of the importance of effort, or persistence.
Support a positive view of one's own ethnicity, which is associated with academic success (d = 0.32), better developmental adjustment (0.40), less delinquency (-0.23) and improved sociability (0.30).

Flag the absence of any meta-analysis of ethnicity and achievement, and note that where ethnicity was used as a moderator the effect sizes for African American and white students were largely the same.

Treat anxiety as a real depressant of performance (about d = -0.43), with worry worse than emotionality and test anxiety (-0.46) worse than general anxiety (-0.32), and note that its consequence can be avoiding the subject entirely.

Report physical and medical influences at their measured size: pre-term birth weight relates to cognitive scores but is confounded by socioeconomic, nutritional and family factors, and chronic illness effects are negative but small (about d = -0.20), differ little across illnesses and may partly reflect absence.

Reject removal of artificial food colours and flavours as a hyperactivity intervention: the treatment effects were barely above chance and diet interventions have limited effect on behaviour despite favourable public reception.
Treat physical and dietary influences as weak: removing artificial food colours 0.12, relaxation 0.16, absence of chronic illness 0.20, physical fitness or exercise 0.25 to 0.36.

Protect physical education: adding it produced small positive academic gains through better concentration, memory and classroom behaviour, and taking curriculum time from other subjects to do so did not reduce achievement in those subjects.

State the limits of stimulant medication precisely: it affects behaviour far more than achievement, works better on lower-level tasks than on reading or mathematics, and shows larger gains on classroom tests than on standardized achievement tests.

Keep the conditionals in the medication chain: drugs may reduce behaviour problems, reduced problems may make a student more attentive, an attentive student may learn — and refuse the straight causal claim that drops them.
Note that reduced behaviour problems under medication were reported by teachers and parents but not by the students themselves or by independent observers, so the rater is part of the finding.

Prefer school-based programmes to drug treatment for attention difficulties (d = 0.58), with contingency management (0.94) and academic interventions (0.69) ahead of cognitive-behavioural procedures (0.19).

Challenge achievement-gap talk that names only below-mean gaps for students of colour, since gaps exist for every ethnicity both above and below the mean and generalizing implies all such students sit at the bottom of the distribution.

Design early intervention and preschool provision to be structured and intense, with about fifteen or more children and up to roughly thirteen hours a week, expecting the benefit to accrue equally for regular, at-risk, disabled and special-education students.

Plan for fade-out: early intervention gains largely disappear after about 60 months for disadvantaged populations, so they are only maximised with systematic, sustained and continuing attention to learning afterwards.
Run study-skills interventions long enough for un-learning: short ones lasting a few days produce the smallest and sometimes negative effects for older students with ingrained habits.
Do not justify early intervention on parental involvement, for which there is little support; do note the strong support for disadvantaged, lower-socioeconomic and minority children gaining the most.

Treat only-born children as indistinguishable from firstborns and children of small families, with achievement motivation the main discriminator against larger families and greater parental attention the likely reason.

Disaggregate parental involvement before recommending it: a surveillance approach produces negative effects, involvement in early intervention produces low effects, and only parental aspirations, expectations and active engagement in the learning produce high effects.

Time parental-involvement effort to the early years: the effect is largest from kindergarten to grade 3 (d = 0.41), declines through grades 3 to 5 (0.36) and reaches roughly zero by secondary school (-0.05).

Prioritise length of participation over earliness of start: there is little evidence that starting earlier is better, while effects are greater for children in a programme at least a year and higher still for minority students.

Sustain openness to experience deliberately, since unlike other traits it does not increase after students leave compulsory schooling even though it is one of the more powerful influences on achievement throughout.

Track the collapse of aspiration over schooling: in one low-socioeconomic community 98 per cent of parents rated education very or extremely important at entry and two-thirds expected diplomas or degrees, yet by the end of elementary school they wanted only a job.

Target successive processing skills — seriation, decoding sequences, working from parts to the whole — in early intervention, since they receive a major boost there and confer an advantage entering formal schooling.

Distinguish active teaching from transmission or frontal instruction, which pitches at middle to high achievers while pacing on feedback from low achievers, under-stimulating fast achievers and frustrating low ones.

Rank home influences correctly: socioeconomic status and home environment highest (both d = 0.57), then parental involvement (0.51) and home visiting (0.29), with family structure (0.17), welfare status (-0.12) and television (-0.18) far lower.

Target the socio-psychological environment and intellectual stimulation of the home — maternal involvement, variety of experience, play materials — rather than socioeconomic indicators such as parental occupation and education.

Suspect parental characteristics behind television effects: parents who allowed unrestricted unsupervised viewing held fewer expectations and lower educational aspirations, and the displacement hypothesis found no support while pro-social effects (d = 0.63) outweighed anti-social ones (0.30).

Expect home visiting to deliver modest cognitive gains generally (d = 0.18) but much larger social-behavioural gains for learning-disabled students (1.01), driven by improvements in parenting (1.06) and parent social functioning (1.52).
Attribute home influence to the beliefs and expectations of the adults rather than to family structure — single or two parents, resident or non-resident father, divorce, adoption, only child.

Place home influences accurately: home environment and socioeconomic status rank 31st and 32nd (0.57 each) alongside strong teaching influences, while parental involvement is 45th (0.51) and home visiting 89th (0.29).

Do not decompose socioeconomic status into one dominant driver: parental education (0.60), income (0.58) and occupation (0.56) behave almost identically and the relationship holds across verbal, mathematics and science achievement.
Account for the language gap children bring: roughly 2.5 million words spoken by school entry for lower socioeconomic groups against about 4.5 million for higher ones.

Report whole language as near-zero on word recognition (0.17) and comprehension (0.09), with low socioeconomic status children given basal readers consistently outperforming those given whole language.

Frame school funding as adequacy — sufficient resource for optimal achievement at a school serving poorer students — rather than as equity that smooths family-level differences while ignoring the school's added load, because SES matters more at school than individual level.

Discount the small measured finance effect appropriately: most studies come from well-resourced countries with small between-school variance, most school money is tied up in fixed costs, and composition effects that matter sit within schools while most analysis is between them.
Note that financial incentives attach to school rather than teacher differences, leaving few incentives for an individual teacher to maximise achievement.

Use home-school liaison to teach parents the language of schooling: a five-year project in low-socioeconomic schools raised engagement and reading achievement and lifted parents' skills, expectations and satisfaction, with effects generally d = 0.30 to 0.60.

Reduce the barrier between school and home, because a child forced to operate in two worlds with two languages finds it harder to build a reputation as a learner, to seek help and to stay open to learning experiences.

Choose tutoring (d = 0.49) or home visits with teacher interaction (0.48) over parent training (0.15) as the form of involvement, and expect far larger effects in reading (0.40) than mathematics (0.18).

Expect technology-based home-school programmes to produce small effects (reading 0.10, mathematics 0.18, writing 0.34) with little evidence of enhanced communication or parental involvement affecting learning.

Do not treat welfare receipt or family structure as explanations for achievement: welfare status has close to zero effect and family structure effects (d = 0.17 overall) are small compared with other influences.
Reject maternal employment as an achievement factor (r = 0.032), with no difference by socioeconomic status, ethnicity, child's age, family structure, or part-time versus full-time work.
Note that the single-parent achievement gap is smallest where family policy is generous — financial assistance, universal child benefits, tax benefits, maternity leave — and largest where it lags.
Report the divorce effect as small and shrinking (from about d = -0.23 in older studies to -0.12 more recently), with teachers seeing essentially no difference and the effect larger for girls.

Expect age at adoption to moderate the achievement effect — no difference in the first year (d = 0.09), growing in the second (0.32) and beyond (0.42), and larger where abuse, neglect or malnourishment preceded adoption (0.46).

Read the television relationship as non-linear rather than uniformly negative: up to roughly two hours a day the association is small and positive, beyond that it turns negative and strengthens up to about 35 to 40 hours a week.
Note that the harmless viewing threshold falls with age — by about seven it is one hour and by seventeen effectively zero — and that adverse effects were greater for females and high-IQ students.

Warn against parental supervision as a lever: monitoring homework, television time and going out had a negative effect on adolescent educational aspirations, and the family behaviours relating negatively to achievement are external rewards, homework surveillance, negative control and restrictions imposed for unsatisfactory grades.

Rank the parental behaviours by effect: participation (d = 0.56) and supportive parenting (0.43) far ahead of homework supervision (0.19), school activities (0.14), communicating with the school (0.14), monitoring progress (0.12), home structure (0.00) and a controlling disciplining style (-0.09).
Advise parents to support autonomous student behaviour rather than to give direct instructional involvement, which relates negatively to achievement.
Avoid or mitigate the negative influences: student mobility (-0.34), television (-0.18), retention (-0.16), welfare policies (-0.12) and summer vacation (-0.09).

Work the expectation chain: higher parental hopes for educational attainment raise the student's own expectations and ultimately their achievement, assisted by parent-student communication and by the student having control over their own studies.

Treat parental expectations as dominating all other parental behaviours — d = 0.58 against 0.21 for school involvement, and d = 0.88 for secondary students against 0.32 for checking homework, 0.14 for attending functions and effectively zero for household rules.

Partner with parents to make their expectations appropriately high and challenging and then work with home and child to realize or surpass them, because alienation of home from school erodes the expectations parents start with.
Communicate from the first day of school high expectations that students will self-regulate and take charge of their own behaviour and academic engagement.

Treat the expenditure-achievement relationship as minimal — across 23 countries the correlation between per-pupil high-school spending and mathematics scores was r = 0.06 — with the most positive relationship running through instructional costs.

Shift the funding question from amount to use: money is too often added with little attention to the efficiency or effectiveness of the resulting outcomes, and the productive question is how it makes a difference above and beyond the fixed costs of running a school.
Ask what the best use of a resource is, or what could be accomplished if the money were spent on innovations with higher effects on student outcomes.
Treat the charter-school advantage as unproven: d = 0.20 dropped to zero once lower-quality studies were excluded, and only eight of 38 states with charter laws had usable independent evaluations.

Warn that summer school widens rather than closes the gap: its small gains (about d = 0.23) are larger for middle-class than disadvantaged students and larger for high than low achievers, though it is usually justified by helping marginal students.

Do not expect summer-school design to rescue the outcome: purpose, curriculum linkage, monitoring, teacher training, use of the school's own teachers, food provision, class size and total hours all produced similar small effects.

Treat school size as curvilinear with an optimum around 600 to 900 students: both much smaller and much larger schools reduce effectiveness, and consolidating very small high schools matters more than consolidating large ones.
Adjust the optimal school size to the cohort: the more affluent the student body the larger the optimum, and the higher the proportion of minority students the smaller it becomes.

Report summer loss at its measured size — d = -0.09 overall, slightly larger in mathematics (-0.14) than reading (-0.05), growing with grade level — and note that middle-class students gained on reading recognition (0.13) while lower-class students lost (-0.14).

Do not expect compensatory funding programmes to close the achievement gap: they raise achievement only slightly (0.12), work better as early rather than later remediation, and lose ground over the summer relative to non-participants.

Note the exchange rate: to match the achievement benefit of increased textbook availability at equal cost, schools would have to cut average class size from 40 to 10, so lowering class size to raise achievement is in most situations not an efficient strategy.

Check article-selection method before crediting a desegregation effect: the better-designed quasi-experiments give considerably smaller effects, falling from about d = 0.45 to 0.20 once selection problems are removed.
Assess desegregation by the opportunities and diversity it provides rather than by its achievement effects, since factors other than classroom composition matter more to achievement.

Treat student mobility as the most negative school influence (d = -0.34), affecting reading and mathematics alike, and note it is any change of school that penalises — the effect is unrelated to number of moves, socioeconomic status or ethnicity.
Recover summer losses by attending to the proficiencies students actually bring back in the first month rather than by extending the school year.

Manage newcomer friendships actively, because the mobility penalty runs through peer effects and disrupted friendships that support learning, and the key success factor at any transition is whether the child makes a friend in the first month.

Discount out-of-school and after-school tutoring (d = 0.09) against what effective teachers achieve in regular classrooms, while noting that shorter programmes and one-on-one tutoring (d = 0.50 in reading) do better than long or group formats.

Treat teacher assignment as most consequential in low-socioeconomic schools, where teacher effects are much larger, and note effectiveness varies more for mathematics (11 per cent) than reading (7 per cent).
Use peer tutoring as a supplement to teacher roles rather than a substitute (d = 0.96 supplemental against 0.63 substitution).
Prefer cross-age tutors (d = 0.79) to same-age peers (0.52) and adult tutors (0.54) in mathematics.

Rank the elementary reforms by cost-effectiveness: cross-age tutoring most cost-effective, computer-assisted instruction mid-range, and a longer school day and reducing class size by five students the smallest returns.

Choose instructional over transformational leadership for student outcomes (d = 0.55 against 0.09): a learning climate free of disruption, clear teaching objectives, and high expectations for teachers and students.

Prioritise the leadership dimensions by effect: promoting and participating in teacher learning (d = 0.91), planning coordinating and evaluating teaching through classroom visits and feedback (0.74), strategic resourcing aligned to teaching priorities (0.60), establishing goals and expectations (0.54), and protecting teaching time (0.49).

Concentrate leadership influence, learning and relationships on the core business of teaching and learning; transformational leadership's generic focus on leader-follower relations is the likely reason for its weaker student effect.

Evaluate leadership style separately for teacher satisfaction and for student achievement, since transformational leadership relates very strongly to job satisfaction (r = 0.71) and is what teachers prefer while doing little for student outcomes.
Treat school leadership as acting on learning indirectly rather than as a direct lever, since principals and school leaders rank 74th (0.36), below classroom-level influences.

Require the five highest-influence leadership behaviours: creating a conversation that challenges the achievement status quo, supplying current and diverse ways to address it, involving teachers in designing and implementing improvement, setting challenging achievement goals, and monitoring the use of feedback about student progress and teaching effectiveness.

Combine high dominance — clarity of purpose and strong guidance — with high cooperation, meaning concern for others' needs and opinions and a desire to work as part of a team, since the relationship powerfully moderates classroom management (d = 0.87).

Concentrate school-level effort on classroom climate, peer influences, absence of disruptive students, curricula made appropriately challenging through acceleration or differentiated gifted provision, and principals acting as instructional leaders — and away from mainstreaming, ability grouping, class size, open classrooms, multi-grade classes, summer courses, retention and mobility.

In leadership assessment weight organizational ability and written communication, which predict enhanced student outcomes, over transformational criteria such as sensitivity, range of interests and personal motivation, which had almost no effect on job performance; neither gender nor ethnicity affected assessment scores.

Prefer goal setting (d = 0.22) and team building (0.30) among organizational development interventions and avoid technostructural ones such as job redesign and job enrichment, and note that organic management shows almost no evidence of positive effects on achievement.
Judge class-size reduction as too small relative to other available interventions to justify its cost, while recognising the positive sign still means increasing class size is poor policy.

Attribute the weak class-size result to teachers carrying on with the methods they used in larger classes, so the smaller class creates an opportunity that is never exploited; smaller classes affect teacher and student work-related conditions more than learning.
Do not promise that other powerful influences will work better in smaller classes: where class sizes were smaller and those influences were implemented, outcomes still did not differ greatly.

Explain that reducing class size only raises the probability that the environment can be structured to capitalize on teaching and peer influences, and that in practice teachers often change nothing about interactions, curricula or strategies.
Answer the probabilistic defence of class-size reduction with the actual question: why the expected benefits of more feedback and individualization do not accrue when class sizes fall.

Cost class-size reduction fully: halving from 30 to 15 yields only d = 0.10 to 0.20, and the true cost includes extra classrooms, resources, ongoing professional development and finding the additional qualified teachers, not just staffing.

Treat a change of class-size band as demanding a re-conceptualization of teaching excellence — from transmitting content to self-regulated learners at 80 or more, through script-following and uniform pacing at 30 to 80, to grouping, peer interaction and tailored curriculum at 20 to 30 — rather than a tweak of method.
Do not stop at forming groups: for grouping to be maximally effective the instructional materials and the teaching must be varied and made appropriately challenging for each group's level.
Have teachers stop over-emphasizing ability and emphasize progress instead, treating a steep learning curve as the right of every student regardless of starting point.
Target mathematics innovations at lower-ability students, at reducing cognitive load, and at feedback flowing both from teacher to student and student to teacher, where their effects are largest.

Raise the frequency of different opportunities rather than total time: teachers should increase the rate of correct academic responses to deliberate practice opportunities until mastery levels defined by the success criteria are met.
Treat class management, optimizing peer co-teaching, and capitalizing on similarities as well as differences as the load-bearing skills, since students are taught in classes of 20 or more.

Copy what schools that doubled performance did: set high goals such as 90 to 95 per cent proficiency, analyze student data deeply, use formative assessment, collectively review evidence on good instruction, use time productively, and provide instructional leadership.
Treat open versus traditional classroom organization as making essentially no difference (d = 0.01), and never read an architectural label as evidence that the practice it names is present.

Identify what actually distinguished effective open-education programmes — emphasis on the child's role in learning, diagnostic evaluation, manipulative materials and individualized instruction — and note that multi-age grouping, open space and team teaching distinguished nothing.
Expect a trade-off: programmes very effective for non-achievement outcomes produced smaller than average effects on academic achievement, so gains on attitude and self-concept can cost attainment.
Reject as not credible that single preferences such as snacking while learning or sitting up straight explain more achievement variance than the major instructional influences.

Set expectations low for comprehensive reform: even the best-evidenced programmes produce small effects (Direct Instruction 0.21, School Development 0.18, Success for All 0.18) and several widely adopted programmes sit at or below zero.
Expect simulation and gaming to deliver only a small positive effect over alternatives (0.12 to 0.38, or 0.32 against lectures alone) and much more on attitude (0.64) than achievement.

Judge tracking on equity as well as achievement: it combines minimal achievement effects with profound negative equity effects, limiting the opportunities, achievements and life chances of students outside the highest tracks, who meet fewer intellectual challenges, less engaging classrooms and fewer well-trained teachers.
Match the outcome measure to the outcome claimed, since a teacher-quality effect can be invisible on a state test that targets surface features while the advantage lies in deeper understanding.

State that evidence is not neutral: what counts as effective depends on judgments about what is educationally desirable, and achievement is only one among other critical outcomes such as affective, persistence, physical and social outcomes.
Expect ability grouping to shape friendship networks around track membership and polarize attitudes, with high-track students growing more enthusiastic and low-track students more alienated.

Audit track placement for social advantage: minority students were seven times more likely to be identified as low- than high-ability, Asian students reached advanced courses more often than Hispanic students with equivalent scores, and advantaged families managed their way into higher tracks.

Inspect low-track classrooms directly: they have been found to be deadening holding tanks with teaching reduced to dull repetitious seatwork and tacit agreements between teachers and students not to push each other.

Resolve the tracking conundrum to teaching quality rather than structure: the near-zero measured effect sits alongside sharply different teaching in low and high tracks, so the key issues are the quality of teaching and the nature of student interaction, not the compositional structure of classes.

Note that detracking is concentrated in low-achieving, poor and urban schools while wealthy suburban schools embrace tracking, which cuts against the account of elites imposing a counterproductive policy on others.

Use within-class grouping selectively: it gives a modest advantage over no grouping (d = 0.17 to 0.25) benefiting all ability levels, but the gain is largest in classes above 35 students (0.35) and close to nothing in classes of 26 to 35 (0.06).

Prefer small groups working cooperatively (d = 0.28) to other small groups (0.15), and expect small-group instruction to gain more against traditional whole-class teaching (0.24) than against individualized mastery learning (0.15).
For gifted students choose acceleration (d = 0.84) over enrichment (0.39) and ability grouping (0.30), noting it is the least implemented of the three.

Note that grouping practices rank poorly throughout: small group learning 48th (0.49), ability grouping for gifted students 87th (0.30), within-class grouping 116th (0.16), ability grouping 121st (0.12) and multi-grade classes 131st (0.04).

Require the conditions that make small-group learning work: prior group-work experience or instruction, specific cooperative learning strategies, and a small group; without them the arrangement does not deliver.
Guarantee the minimum conditions for learning: time on task, exposure to teaching, collaborative practice between teacher and student, and opportunities to practice.
Give students group-work training and explicit cooperative structures before small-group computer work, which significantly enhances it.

Read least restrictive environment as modification of content, materials, classroom management, instructional techniques and strategies — not as simply placing a student with disabilities in a regular class.

Individualize disability instruction by affected processes, strengths, context, and co-occurring needs; for supported children, favor deep intensive strategy teaching, monitoring, cues, supervised practice, feedback, and small-group interaction.

Report mainstreaming at its measured size: small positive advantages over special classes (about d = 0.08 to 0.15), larger for students classified as mentally retarded (0.47) than learning disabled (0.13).

Use systematic formative evaluation by teachers, which raises achievement for students with mild learning disability (d = 0.70) and works across student age, treatment duration, measurement frequency and special-needs status.
Note that breadth of reform does not predict impact: comprehensive interventions for learning disabled students rank 7th (0.77) while comprehensive teaching reforms rank 105th (0.22).

Know the top ten: self-reported grades (1.44), Piagetian programs (1.28), providing formative evaluation (0.90), micro teaching and acceleration (0.88), classroom behavioural interventions (0.80), comprehensive interventions for learning disabled students (0.77), teacher clarity (0.75), reciprocal teaching (0.74) and feedback (0.73).

Expect retention damage to compound: retained students were 0.45 standard deviations behind their promoted comparison group after one year and 0.83 behind four or more years later, even though the promoted group was tested on more advanced material.

Expect diminishing returns from test frequency: students taking at least one test in a 15-week term scored about half a standard deviation above those taking none, and many short tests beat few long ones on identical items.
Treat retention as the second greatest predictor of drop-out: being retained once almost doubles the likelihood of dropping out and failing twice almost guarantees it.
Attribute retention's harm to repeating a programme that already failed the child with no special intervention, and to peer-group effects of working with students of a different age.

Answer the social objection to acceleration with the evidence: accelerated gifted students showed slightly positive social effects (d = 0.13) with negative effects for those not accelerated, so the question is what social harm follows from failing to accelerate.
Combine modeling, coaching and reinforcement and target the student's specific identified deficit directly, while acknowledging that persistence of the effect over time remains problematic.
Weigh a small positive effect against the counterfactual: without the compensatory programme, the children served over thirty years would have fallen further behind academically.
Audit retention for equity: given two students of the same achievement, the student of colour is about four times more likely to be retained, and those held back are more likely to be poor and male.
Reject the threat of non-promotion as a motivator and treat retention as a poor use of the education dollar, adding an extra year of cost without benefit for the vast majority.
Set the operational demand: schools should enhance learning by at least d = 0.30 more than last year and preferably more than 0.40 before an intervention is considered worth retaining.

Distinguish gifted programmes from high-ability tracks: tracks give a faster pace and harder tasks within the same curriculum, while it is specific curricula aimed at challenging students at the appropriate level that make engagement and learning more likely.

Treat enrichment as at best deferring boredom, since no study has shown it superior to acceleration; where it is used, mastering more mature ideas outperforms broader sweeps through the regular curriculum, and it works far better in mathematics (1.10) and science (1.23) than reading (0.59) or social studies (0.23).
Choose meta-cognitive strategies (0.96) over cognitive acceleration (0.61) and instrumental enrichment (0.58) among thinking-skill programmes.
Staff enrichment with teachers experienced in working with gifted students: experienced teachers achieved d = 0.88 while those with no or limited experience achieved d = -0.06.

Expect accomplished teaching to shift the depth of student work rather than test scores: about 74 per cent of certified teachers' work samples showed deep understanding against 29 per cent for non-certified, while the writing achievement difference was slight.

Do not expect mentoring to move performance (d = 0.08 to 0.18) though it moves attitudes more (satisfaction 0.6), because it is an apprentice model of social and role-model experience involving little teaching.
Look for expertise effects in the depth of student work: 74 per cent of certified teachers' student work was judged deep against 29 per cent for non-certified teachers.

Among management methods use disciplinary interventions that signal whether behaviour is appropriate (d = 1.00), group contingency strategies (0.98), tangible recognition (0.82) and direct concrete consequences (0.57).
Negotiate rules and procedures with students rather than imposing them, since stated, well-articulated and negotiated expectations raise achievement (d = 0.76).
Require expectations that are challenging, appropriate to the student, and checkable against what is deemed valuable, rather than left implicit.

Treat reducing disruptive behaviour as a core competency of any successful teacher, aiming not to remove the disruptive student — who is often less disruptive in a different class — but to ensure no student needlessly disrupts their own or others' learning.

Choose behavioural over non-behavioural interventions against disruption (d = 0.76 against 0.35), with social or token reinforcement (1.38), behavioural consultation (1.09), cooperation (1.05) and cognitive behaviour modification (1.0) ahead of social skills training (0.44).
Target academic outcomes when working with disruptive students, since programmes doing so had greater effect than those targeting classroom behaviour or social interactions.
Use direct behavioural observation rather than teacher rating scales to evaluate a disruption intervention, since rating-scale studies were less likely to show reductions.

Treat the damage from an ineffective teacher as persistent and class-wide: it is measurable in later years' achievement, shows little compensatory recovery from more effective teachers in subsequent grades, and applies to all students in that teacher's class.
Treat communicating lesson intentions and what success looks like as a load-bearing teacher behaviour, not a presentational nicety.

Stop depending on a small number of key students as indicators, which leaves teachers ignorant of what most of the class knows and sustained by the belief that engagement in appropriate activities implies learning.
Identify the real problem as the average get-through-the-curriculum, behave, be busy teacher who has no idea of the damage being done, not the criminal or incompetent one.
Attend to friendship quality from early adolescence, when its influence on achievement is strongest and the reputations it confers can help or harm academic achievement.
Justify social skills programmes by the social outcome they actually move: strong on peer relations (0.80 to 0.90) and social outcomes (0.5 to 0.6) but weak on academic achievement (0.10 to 0.20).
Treat giving each student a friend as a direct route to raising academic achievement, since under cooperative conditions interpersonal relations have the strongest influence on it.

Watch the direction of peer influence: friendship supports well-being, school belonging, sense of worth and positive feelings toward school, but does the opposite where the peer group signals that learning is not valued.

Treat low classroom peer acceptance as a learning problem, not only a social one, because exclusion restricts access to the social and instrumental resources carried in class peer activities and links consistently to disengagement and lower achievement.
Do not treat structured peer tutoring (0.76) and unstructured peer group work (0.15) as the same intervention.

Guard against the second harm of exclusion: students who cannot participate for cultural or ethnic reasons not only miss the knowledge but learn that their ability to acquire knowledge is inferior, a deficit belief teachers can reinforce by sharing it.

Reject school uniform and dress-code policies as achievement or safety interventions: no effect at elementary level, a significant negative effect at high school, and no effect on attendance, self-esteem, locus of control, coping, drug use or behaviour incidents.

Separate working conditions from achievement: working conditions are worth pursuing in their own right, but focusing on them displaces debate about the matters that actually affect student achievement.

Note that students typically name only two or three of the 40 to 60 teachers they encounter as having made a real difference, and that the ones they name turned them on to the love and challenge of the subject.
Expect students describing their best teachers to name relationship building, different and better strategies for learning the subject, and willingness to explain material and help with their work.

Recognise which teachers students remember: those who cared about teaching them a passion for the subject, gave them confidence in themselves as learners and people, treated them as a person, and instilled a love of learning — not those who covered a syllabus.
Note that the most effective teachers are often not the ones parents pick as better, but the students know them and welcome being in their classes.

Read the certified-over-emergency advantage as accumulated pedagogical content knowledge rather than subject-matter knowledge, since it rises to d = 0.39 only when the certified group also has several years of experience.

Reinstate microteaching and laboratory experience — mini-lessons to a small group, videotaped, followed by analysis and debriefing — which produce moderate to strongly positive effects (d = 0.70 to 0.88) that do not significantly decay, yet are far less used today.
Challenge teacher programmes that train low-level skills reinforcing what the trainee already does, with too little exposure to new conceptions and new ways of teaching.

Require the seven features of exemplary teacher education: coherence around a clear vision of good teaching, well-defined standards guiding coursework and clinical work, curriculum grounded in development learning social context and subject pedagogy, extended clinical experience interwoven with coursework, explicit strategies for confronting deep-seated beliefs, shared knowledge and beliefs among all who teach the trainees, and assessment through performance demonstrations and portfolios.

Reintroduce micro-skills teaching methods, build understanding of how to teach surface, deep and conceptual knowledge distinctly, and show how student assessment feeds back to the teacher on who was not taught well and what needs re-teaching.
Train teachers in questioning, which is highly open to change through training and yields achievement gains.
Require knowledge, empathy and verbal ability together, since they are greater than the sum of the parts and effectiveness drops by more than a third if one is missing.
Track out-of-field teaching as a real risk: about a fifth of teachers were not certified in the subject they taught, far worse in some sciences, and teaching in field carries a measurable advantage.

Expect interpersonal skills training in pre-service to raise new teachers' positive attitudes and self-concepts (d = 0.30) but to decline once teachers begin work, particularly in inner-city schools where they were less well prepared.

Expect social skills programmes to work least well for the students they most target: effects drop to about d = 0.20 for students identified as social problems or with emotional, behavioural or learning disorders.
Define quality teaching as students rate it — challenging students, holding high expectations, encouraging engagement with the subject, and valuing both surface and deep aspects of it.
Rank the teacher's contributions: quality of the teacher and the nature of teacher-student relationships largest, expectations and professional development medium, teacher education programs low.
Reframe teacher-quality discussion from personal and professional attributes to the quality of effects on learning, making teaching the more critical object of discussion than teachers.
Put the leverage in teaching rather than structures: active quality teaching strategies average d = 0.68 against 0.08 for working conditions.

Read a teaching rating as measuring partly presentation, not solely learning: instructor expressiveness moves ratings substantially but achievement only slightly, while lecture content moves achievement substantially but ratings only slightly.

Pair rating feedback with consultation rather than merely delivering it, since feedback from student ratings makes only a medium contribution to improving teaching (d = 0.38) and the effect is amplified by consultation.
Measure teacher clarity through student rather than observer rating, since effects are larger that way, and note that class size and subject taught make no difference to it.

Judge a curriculum review by whether it changes instructional strategy: content matters less than the strategies teachers use to move students upward through it, and a review that changes content alone will not move learning.

Collect student evaluations in elementary and high schools rather than relying on the belief that quality is high or that students are too immature to judge, because students sit in the classes and know whether the teacher sees learning through their eyes.

Check the class-wide expectation level rather than expectations towards particular groups, since expectation effects depend less on student attributes such as gender or race than on whether the expectation is held high or low for all students.
Scrutinize the teacher's lens, consider it from another's viewpoint, and check it against evidence that all students are learning desirable outcomes at a sufficient rate.

Treat conflicting evidence on board certification honestly: large-scale growth comparisons report effects near zero (d = 0.04 to 0.05) while others report small to moderate gains (0.09 to 0.43 by subject).

Use the three discriminators of accomplished teaching: systematically and consistently setting appropriately challenging goals through demanding engaging assignments (d = 1.37), testing hypotheses about the effects of one's own teaching (1.09), and holding a deeper understanding of that teaching and its effects (1.02).

Invest in person-centered teaching, which correlates 0.34 (d = 0.72) with achievement and attitude outcomes across 119 studies and 355,325 students, most strongly with critical and creative thinking and least with grades.
Ask what the minimum subject knowledge is to be an accomplished teacher and how to optimize the teaching strategies of those who have more, rather than whether more is better.

Require students to be both physically and mentally engaged for active construction of meaning, with teacher questioning, focusing and manipulation strategies around d = 0.57 to 0.58 and instructional media lowest at 0.18.

Rank the teaching approaches: providing formative evaluation (0.90) and feedback (0.73) highest, then spaced practice (0.71) and meta-cognitive strategies (0.69), with student control over learning (0.04), mentoring (0.15) and individualized instruction (0.23) lowest.
Treat challenge as relative to the student's current performance and to the success criteria derived from the learning intention, not as an absolute property of the task.

Centre the account on passionate accomplished teachers who focus on students' cognitive engagement with the content, developing ways of thinking, reasoning, problem solving and strategies within that content.
Define accomplished teachers as those who systematically make these differences — engaging students, turning them on to the subject, inspiring them and communicating a passion for learning.

Note that direct, actively involved teaching with a high sense of agency produces higher levels of learning, autonomy and self-regulation — the very outcomes unguided methods claim as their rationale.

Do explicit teaching and reteaching of skills — modeling and explaining, then guided student practice — and expect scaffolding and reteaching to account for a large proportion of an effective teacher's effort.

Make teacher assignment a policy lever rather than an administrative detail, since raising achievement for all requires reducing the chance that any student is assigned to a relatively ineffective teacher.

Require any professional development claim to state which of the four outcome levels it was measured at — reaction, teacher learning, teacher behaviour, student outcomes — since most evaluations report changes in teachers rather than impact on students.
Expect professional development effects to decay across the chain: teacher learning d = 0.90, teacher behaviour 0.60, teacher reactions 0.42, student learning only 0.37.
Use student report as an instrument for detecting expectancy effects, since students accurately perceive differential treatment and can report which teachers favour some children over others.

Evaluate a teacher education programme on the appropriateness of its articulated graduating standards and the quality of evidence that all its students meet them, with employers and independent educationalists sitting alongside the programme's own academics.
Know the expected success criteria and what students will be accountable for, and inform students of those standards of performance.
Spread professional development over an extended period, except where a single powerful idea grounds new practice and independently produces high impact on student outcomes.

Involve external experts, secure school leadership support, provide access to relevant expertise and allow time to process new information, all of which raise professional development effectiveness above within-school initiatives alone.

Require the key components of effective comprehensive reform: ongoing professional development, measurable goals and benchmarks for student learning, a faculty vote securing buy-in, specific innovative curricular materials, and instructional practices designed to improve teaching and learning.
Secure commitment to the teaching strategy and re-learning of how to use it through professional development, since it is differences in teachers that make the difference in student learning.
Do not read funding, release time or voluntary versus compulsory participation as quality signals: they are unrelated to professional development's influence on student outcomes.
Cite the Pygmalion bloomers finding as suggestive rather than established, given many failed replications and documented methodological problems.

Expect teachers to obtain the outcomes they expect regardless of whether the expectation is accurate, since interpersonal expectancy effects average d = 0.70 across 345 experiments and are as large in everyday situations as in the laboratory.
Attribute the above-average effect to teachers using particular methods, holding high expectations for all students, and having built positive relationships — not to teachers as a category.

Expect laboratory experience to raise manipulation skills (d = 1.26) far more than concepts and subject learning (0.33) and barely to touch reasoning (0.06), which explains why heavy laboratory emphasis can lower overall outcomes.
Judge feedback by content rather than frequency, timing or positive-versus-negative valence, since routine praise or bare correction carries no information beyond right-or-wrong.

Supply teachers with pertinent academic information about students, which reduces the weight placed on irrelevant cues such as attractiveness — markedly reduced though not eliminated when explicit competence evidence is present.

Show teachers survey evidence of student perceptions, since teachers routinely misjudge their relationships by assuming they are positive and looking for confirming cues, and such evidence prompts rapid change in practice.
Make seeking surprising evidence the working defence against negative expectation effects: teachers should look for evidence that disconfirms their prior expectations and be prepared to be surprised.
Locate teacher harm in expectation rather than in generally harmful teachers: few teachers actively decrease achievement, but low expectations held for a whole class systematically depress it.
Do not cite a labeling study as evidence about achievement: most measure how teachers and parents differentiate labeled from regular students rather than what those students attain.

Locate mathematics disability in verbal working memory rather than numerical ability, since the largest deficits are in verbal problem solving (d = -0.58), naming speed and verbal word memory (-0.70 each).

Treat low achievers and reading-disabled students as sharing a common phonological processing problem: they do not differ in automaticity (d = -0.06) or real-word reading (0.02), so the disability label does not identify a distinct reading mechanism.
Use problem-solving teaching (d = 0.61), expecting a much larger effect on verbal flexibility (0.81) than figural flexibility (0.40).

Assess mathematics disability across fact retrieval, procedure execution and sequencing, spatial representation, number processing, errors, and working-memory demands—not low achievement or strategy choice alone.
Give phonics training to students with low reading achievement or an identified reading disability, since it directly raises achievement, particularly spelling and word recognition.
Treat reading acumen by mid-elementary as a cross-curricular gate, since schooling shifts early from learning to read to reading to learn and a student without it is handicapped everywhere.
Configure reading instruction as phonics combined with additional language and literacy activities, with phonics, fluency and comprehension as the core ingredients.
Use direct instruction to teach phonics skills, and combine it with taught word-recognition strategies to improve reading comprehension for students with learning disabilities.
Specifically assess and teach automaticity in word recognition and decoding for learning-disabled students, in whom it does not emerge naturally as it does between second and third grade for others.
Accept that reading method makes little difference to achievement broadly, except for sound-symbol blending, where systematic synthesis of separate letter sounds is superior.

Prefer a bottom-up reading approach emphasizing accurate word recognition, decoding and letter awareness over a top-down approach premised on cognitive and language abilities — while noting direct instruction and strategy training beat both.

Do not let a diagnostic distinction drive teaching: students classified as brain injured differ from those with familial-cultural difficulties by only d = 0.10 across 241 effect sizes, and labels mainly serve to classify students and unlock funding rather than change what works.

Build teacher clarity — organization, explanation, examples, guided practice and assessment of student learning, with clear speech as a prerequisite — which relates to achievement at r = 0.35 (d = 0.75).

Require the effective teacher to hold clear instructional goals communicated to students and parents that address the knowledge domains as well as the cognitive, meta-cognitive and self systems, and to understand the interrelationships among them.

Prefer what teachers do to what teachers hold: teacher training ranks 124th (0.11) and subject matter knowledge 125th (0.09) while teacher clarity ranks 8th (0.75) and professional development 19th (0.62).

Explain the weak subject-knowledge finding as a restriction of range — nearly all teachers clear an acceptable threshold, leaving little variance to detect — rather than as proof that knowledge is irrelevant.
Check prior proficiency before teaching, since half of all material taught in a class is already known by the students and a teacher who does not check spends much of the year on redundant content.
Re-teach before practice if there is any doubt the class has understood, because students must practice doing it right.
Grow a student from where that student actually is, not from where the teacher believes they should be at the start of the year.

Place curricular programmes against the d = 0.45 curricula average, with creativity (0.65), tactile stimulation (0.58), outdoor and adventure (0.52) and play programs (0.50) high, and perceptual-motor (0.08) and extra-curricular programs (0.17) near zero.

Place integrated curricula at elementary (0.56) and middle school (0.57) rather than high school (0.27), with experienced implementers and for lower-achieving and ethnically diverse students, and target the active elements — thematic instruction (0.46) and process skills (0.36) — rather than integration as such.

Make extra-curricular programmes highly organized and structured, regular, building increasingly complex skills and goal setting, and led by one or more competent adults with age-appropriate expectations.

Do not report near transfer as general comprehension improvement: vocabulary instruction gives a large gain on passages containing the taught words (d = 0.97) but only a small gain on global comprehension (0.30).

Use repeated reading for both fluency and comprehension, expecting near transfer to the practised passage (d = 0.76) to exceed far transfer to new passages (0.50) while far transfer remains substantial.
Check the unit of analysis behind a comprehension effect: vocabulary d = 1.77 against reading comprehension 0.70, and word-level units 1.28 against whole-text units 0.82.
Reject incidental acquisition as the vehicle for vocabulary growth: students learn only about 15 per cent of the unknown words they meet during normal reading.

For children with an identified language disorder use a modeling approach rather than focused stimulation or comprehension methods, expecting syntax to improve most and pragmatic language functioning least, and expecting reduced gains where significant neurological impairment is present.
Attribute a language programme's effectiveness to its structured and sequential design rather than to its brand.

Define systematic phonics as a planned, sequenced set of letter-sound correspondences — consonants, short and long vowels, digraphs and letter-sound blends — not incidental exposure to the alphabetic code.
Use letters when manipulating phonemes, and prefer synthetic phonics — converting letters to sounds, blending them into words, then analyzing larger sub-parts — over the alternatives.

Report phonics effects by outcome: d = 0.86 on phonological outcomes, 0.59 on spelling and 0.53 on reading, so the largest effect is on the proximal skill and the reading effect is materially smaller.
Treat phonological awareness training as a causal factor in learning to read (d = 0.73 randomized, 0.70 matched), not merely a correlate.
Check whether the outcome measure was simple decoding or real-word identification before comparing phonological training effects, since the measure inflates or deflates the result.
Read an implausibly large effect as a methodological error rather than a large real effect — d = 22.29, implying a style-achievement correlation of 0.996, is beyond the imaginable.
Narrow rather than expand phonemic-awareness coverage: teaching one or two types produces larger effects than teaching many.
Do not treat delivery mode as the constraint on phonemic awareness: effects hold whether delivered by classroom teachers or computer, and by tutoring, small group or whole class.
Concentrate phonemic awareness work in the learning-to-read phase, since effects are higher for preschool than higher grades and decrease as age increases.
Reject the claim that phonemic awareness instruction disadvantages poorer children: it benefits low socioeconomic status students as much as middle and high status students.
Do not report short-term phonological gains as durable ones: long-term effects are smaller, though phonemic training remains discernible after an average of 18.5 months.
Deliver phonological awareness training in groups rather than individually, and combine phonological with letter training rather than phonological training alone.
Specify dosage as part of the intervention: the most successful phonemic awareness programme targeted word recognition and ran more than 1.5 hours over more than 8 weeks (d = 1.02).
Exclude sentence-combining instruction from the reading toolkit: its effects on comprehension are small and ambiguous, though it is more effective at elementary than high school level.

Build comprehension programmes on processing strategies — inferential reasoning, summarizing rules, text chunking (d = 1.04) — over text-focused (0.77) and task-focused (0.69) designs, for poor and good readers alike.

Attribute comprehension-strategy effects to the teacher explicitly teaching the strategy, not to the materials: both visually dependent (0.94) and language dependent (1.18) strategies work only under that condition.

Note that motivation and strategy instruction can be addressed together: a concept-oriented reading programme pairing comprehension mini-lessons with motivational engagement raised multiple-text comprehension (0.93), fluency (0.73) and self-efficacy (0.49).

Give strategy training — verbal elaboration, mediation, imagery and verbal rehearsal — to all children, since it benefits those with and without intellectual disabilities, and use it for mathematical word problems (0.77) where it also aids maintenance and generalization.
Match text difficulty to the learning goal, since a low density of unknown words yields more incidental word learning than a high density.

Audit how primary studies were coded before treating two syntheses as contradictory: the apparent positive result for whole language rests on classifying as whole language studies that in fact taught phonological recoding, word lists, letter-sound naming and decoding.
Do not report a whole-language attitude gain as a reading-skill gain: it does improve children's attitudes towards reading while remaining negligible for learning to read.
Deliberately teach reading strategies, especially to struggling readers, since whole language may have value for later reading but not for the process of learning to read.

Do not rely on sustained silent reading: it has little effect on reading attitude and none above grade 3, and for students who struggle or dislike reading it becomes another occasion confirming that reading is not enjoyable.
Distinguish who does the reading aloud: teachers using it as a teaching tool produce d = 0.63 on oral language and 0.41 on reading, while volunteers have little or no effect.
Do not use unpaid classroom volunteers to teach reading: there is little good evidence it works and almost half those studies showed negative effects.

Deliver Reading Recovery as a supplement to, not a replacement for, classroom teaching, where it produces large effects for at-risk readers (d = 0.96 overall; comprehension 0.67, decoding 0.56, oral word reading 0.69).
Read aloud to younger children in small groups, since those conditions foster more interaction between reader, child and text.

Promote parent-preschooler joint book reading across all socioeconomic groups (language growth d = 0.67, emergent literacy 0.58, reading achievement 0.55), expecting effects to diminish as children become able to read alone.
State that reading to children is not sufficient to produce competent readers: instruction is also needed, and exposure or practice in listening does not substitute for it.
Attend to all five pillars of reading — phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension — since that matters far more than which single pillar a programme emphasizes.

Order the reading curricula by rank: vocabulary and repeated reading 15th and 16th (0.67), phonics 22nd (0.60), comprehension programs 28th (0.58), exposure to reading 76th (0.36), sentence combining 119th (0.15) and whole language 129th (0.06).

Quantify the method penalty: a teacher using whole language would need to be at least ten times more effective than one using phonics to reach the same outcomes, and a teacher combining vocabulary, phonics and comprehension outperforms either single-method teacher.
Flag that reading research concentrates on the early years with no meta-analyses and only limited evidence beyond them, so recommendations for older readers rest on weaker ground.

Read the upper-elementary pattern as a plateau rather than a slump: more than 80 per cent of year 5 students are at or above expectation, close to half fall below by year 8, and about 80 per cent are above again by year 11.

Import the high-school demands into upper-elementary teaching — finding information, making connections, inferring and understanding within content-area literacy — since reading growth resumes where those demands are made.

Balance skills instruction with holistic reading and writing activities rather than choosing between them, and connect content learning in science, social studies and mathematics to reading and writing instruction.
Teach strategies for planning, revising and editing compositions (d = 0.82), particularly for struggling writers.

Prioritise the writing moves by effect: summarizing strategies (0.82), collaborative planning, drafting, revising and editing (0.75), and clear specific goals for the product (0.70), ahead of word processing (0.55) and sentence-complexity strategies (0.50).
For students with learning disabilities teach the critical steps of the writing process and the conventions of the genre explicitly, with guided feedback and procedural prompts (d = 0.86).
Teach organizing and transforming instructional material first (d = 0.85), such as outlining before writing, followed by self-consequences (0.70), self-instruction and self-evaluation (0.62 each).
Build writing workshops on teams, peer feedback and collaborative authorship, and make the purpose and audience of each piece explicit, since audience and purpose appear to drive the gains.
Use creative drama as an instructional tool principally at preschool and elementary levels (d = 0.48 on cognitive skill acquisition), where it benefits both regular and remedial students.
Use socio-dramatic play with younger children, which is the most effective type against imaginative play as the least, and note that adult-directed play adds nothing over other play conditions.
Treat the proposed mechanisms for music practice improving reading as plausible but unestablished, since causality cannot be determined from the meta-analytic evidence.

Do not use the music and spatial-temporal reasoning association (d = 0.49) to justify instructional practice: it is remarkably variable, at best temporary, and of no established educational importance.
Check the setting behind a pooled effect before reading it as instructional: the very large music effect (d = 2.90) comes substantially from therapy rather than education studies.

Where music is used as a behavioural contingency, expect it to work slightly better at increasing desirable behaviour than reducing undesirable, and use music interruption rather than initiation to establish the contingency.

Do not generalize narrow transfer to broad cognitive gain: transfer from arts study occurs only across a narrow bridge, from visual arts experience to drawing-based tests, and not to generating ideas, concepts or words.
Read the arts-achievement relation as very small (d = 0.10) and non-causal, with the plausible route running through raised engagement in schooling rather than direct cognitive transfer.
Treat manipulatives as neither harmful nor supportive of mathematics learning, with their highest effects on concrete rather than abstract instructional components.
In high school algebra use direct instruction (0.55) and problem solving (0.52) rather than technology-aided or communication and study-skills methods (0.07 each).

For learning-disabled and lower-achieving mathematics students use guided practice (0.86), strategy-based methods (0.85), peer tutoring (0.76) and teacher modeling (0.73), and avoid unstructured peer group work (0.15) and technology for independent practice (0.16).

Use calculators when applied to computation, drill and checking, when they reduce cognitive load so students can attend to concepts, and when they are an integral pedagogical element rather than an add-on.
Target calculator use at lower-ability students (d = 0.30) and withhold it from high-ability students, for whom the effect is negative (-0.23) because the cognitive-load relief is redundant.
Embed the calculator in instruction rather than merely making it available: effects reach d = 0.72 for composition problem solving when it is part of the teaching process.
Match the assessment condition to the instructional condition: allowing calculators during instruction but withholding them at test produces negative effects (d = -0.21).

State the calculator's actual contribution: neither help nor hindrance to overall mathematics achievement, with reduced cognitive load and improved attitude to mathematics (d = 0.37) as the minimum benefit, and larger gains on conceptual (0.72) than procedural (0.52) skills.

Explain calculator problem-solving gains as improved computation and lowered cognitive workload, with the attitude gain likely coming from relieving students' dislike of word problems by removing the need to compute while solving.
Target reading strategy training at lower-ability students (d = 0.89 against 0.71 middle and 0.28 higher), and at high school (0.85) and college (0.62) rather than elementary (0.55).
Use computer work to supplement teacher instruction (0.45) rather than substitute for it (0.30), noting it makes no difference whether the same or a different teacher delivers the two conditions.

Target malleable student states over fixed attributes: concentration and engagement 49th (0.48) and motivation 51st (0.48) against gender 122nd (0.12), personality 109th (0.19), diet 123rd (0.12) and lack of illness 102nd (0.23).

Prefer skills-based science programmes emphasizing analytic and process skills to traditional fact-and-law curricula, which they outperform on attitudes, process skills, analytic skills and achievement, with positive effects on all outcomes except self-concept.
Use laboratory work to question, explain and discover rather than to verify previously presented material (d = 0.57 in favour), since the purpose of the lab and not the lab itself carries the effect.

Check test alignment before crediting a curriculum: effects of innovative science curricula are greatest on innovative and neutral tests and much lower on tests favouring traditional content, so alignment partly manufactures the effect.
Treat downstream continuity as a condition on the claimed benefit, since gains from activity-based elementary science may be lost when students later enter classrooms using traditional methods.

Correct science misconceptions with discussion webs (0.51), learning charts and augmented activation (0.43 each) rather than mere activation of prior knowledge (0.10) or question-answer-explanation (0.02).

Understand moral education as targeting moral judgment rather than achievement (overall d = 0.28), with moral-dilemma discussion (0.41) ahead of personality development (0.36) and effects far larger for adults (0.61) than school students (0.22 to 0.23).
Recognise the moral dimension: the constant need to ask what the desirable outcomes of any teaching are, alongside teachers' judgment proficiency and caring relationships.
Provide social skills training on a regular and sustained basis rather than as a one-off, since gains are mostly short-term with weak long-term effects.

Expect social competence training to move social-cognitive skills most (0.77), social interaction less (0.34) and social adjustment least (0.18), with large effects appearing only when direct goal criteria are the outcome rather than broader constructs.
Do not assume students already possess social skills or would not benefit from systematic intervention, since peer co-learning and reduced disruption depend on those skills.
Make social problem-solving programmes behavioural, include teacher-student dialogue about social problem solving, and run them for 40 lessons or more.

Require teachers to know what each student is thinking and knowing, construct meaningful experiences in light of that, and hold enough content knowledge to give feedback that moves each student progressively through the curriculum levels.

Treat treatment intensity as the only significant contributor to career-counseling outcomes, with class interventions most effective overall but requiring the most hours and individual counseling producing more gain per hour.

Do not expect career education to raise achievement (d = 0.16), and note it does so only for average-ability elementary students when coupled with mathematics and language arts content and run for roughly 151 to 200 hours a year.
Sequence rather than fuse mathematics and science, since the gain accrues to the subject taught last and teaching science before mathematics therefore serves mathematics better.

Reject perceptual motor training: it does not improve academic or cognitive learning (reading -0.04, spelling 0.02, language 0.03, handwriting 0.05, mathematics 0.10), a child given it is likely to gain nothing or lose ground, and the time it consumes is a real cost.

Inspect study quality before believing a positive pooled effect, since in both the perceptual motor and tactile stimulation literatures the weakest designs produced the largest effects and rigorous internal-validity controls produced smaller ones.
Read tactile stimulation of infants as improving social and personal (0.61), physiological (0.54) and motor outcomes (0.53) more than cognitive or language outcomes (0.36).
State play's creativity claim narrowly: it relates only weakly to originality with familiar objects, not at all with unfamiliar objects, and has no effect on problem solving.
