Build creativity programmes on instructional structure rather than free exploration — high structuring (0.80), questioning (0.73) and responding to student questioning (0.70) — an effect constant across all subject areas.
Expect fluency to be easier to improve than originality, and use explicit instruction with a thinking-strategy basis, which makes creativity programmes most successful.

Treat as speculative the possibility that creativity training raises motivation to perform rather than underlying ability, given its gains are enhanced by activities aimed at setting and meeting high expectations.
Do not report a thinking programme's affective gain as a cognitive one: they move affective outcomes (1.44) far more than cognitive outcomes or curricula achievement (0.62 each).
Prefer cognitively based to emotionally or affectively based self-esteem programmes, and note that programmes run by teachers are the least successful.
Note adventure programmes as one of the few interventions with positive follow-up effects (0.17) added on top of end-of-programme effects (0.34), where most interventions show diminishing returns.
Reject change for change's sake, since not all interventions succeed and excellence comes from seeking formative evaluation of a programme's intended and unintended effects.
Do not sum effect sizes: coupling interventions together does not mean their effects can be added, and the adventure-programme additivity was noted as unusual.
Orient adventure programmes to teaching rather than to the outdoor experience, since programmes requiring instructors to hold social science degrees far outperformed experience-oriented ones.

Reproduce the working mechanism of adventure programmes anywhere: very challenging learning intentions with clear success criteria, optimized peer support, and feedback both given throughout and actively sought by participants.
Run outdoor programmes beyond roughly 20 days, since longer programmes are much more successful and younger participants gain more than older ones.
Discount the extra-curricular achievement effect (0.47) as possibly inflated, since it comes from one of the few meta-analyses using a random effects model.
Prefer academic-type extra-curricular activities for achievement: sport contributes little (0.10) and paid work nothing (-0.01) while actually increasing risk behaviours (0.29).

Value sport and work for identity formation and peer self-esteem and for keeping a student in school where the academic dividend is then earned, so a near-zero achievement effect is not the whole value case.

Attribute bilingual programme variation to teaching competence and explicit attention to learning strategies rather than to the bilingual design, noting the programmes pursue heterogeneous goals from immigrant remediation to cultural preservation.

Check the neighbourhood-language confound before crediting a bilingual programme: effects appear positive when experimental and comparison groups share a neighbourhood language but shrink to little difference when the comparison group's is English.

Recognise the cosmetic curriculum change: objectives regrouped under higher-order concepts while fundamental objectives stay put, with the named teaching methods usually passive or constructivist — the least successful ones.
Make second- and third-chance programmes available for students who miss the first time, since they are effective at remediating those deficiencies.

Define strategic teaching as finding ways to engage and motivate students, teaching strategies inside the specific curricula domain rather than generically, and constantly seeking feedback on how effective the teaching is with every student.
Treat test preparation as a poor substitute for instruction: teaching test taking and coaching (0.22) and frequency of testing (0.34) sit well below the d = 0.45 teaching-approach average.
Rule out the competing explanations before crediting a high-stakes testing gain: coaching effects, narrowed curriculum, teaching to the test, and excluding weaker students from the tested population.

Expect interventions for students with learning difficulties to average d = 0.56, with meta-cognitive (0.98), writing and creativity (0.84), reading comprehension (0.82) and memory/recall (0.81) highest and social skills lowest (0.46).
Choose active and guided instruction over unguided facilitative instruction: the teacher as activator averages d = 0.60 against 0.17 for the teacher as facilitator.

Adapt learning intentions so they are appropriate to all students, since not everyone in the class is working at the same level, and vary time by kind of intention — concepts and deeper learning need more time than surface information.
Stay aware of what students learn beyond the stated learning intentions and assess for those unintended consequences rather than against the plan alone.

Share the lesson's learning intentions and notions of success with students rather than keeping them in the lesson plan, since that is when behavioural objectives and advance organizers produce their highest effects.

Accept that some learning is dull and repetitive and must be over-learned to free cognitive resources for anticipation and understanding, and that turning students on to that part requires the same passion.
Do not map learning intentions one-to-one onto activities: one activity can serve several intentions and one intention may need several activities or repeated exposures.
Add an implementation intention in if-then form to every goal (d = 0.65), since the presence of a goal and commitment to it are not sufficient without a plan for how it will be reached.
Vary goal difficulty, not goal specificity: difficulty drives success and the relationship between degree of difficulty and performance is directly linear (pooled d = 0.67).

Quote the size of the goal-difficulty effect: students given the most challenging goals perform over 250 per cent higher than those given the easiest, and difficult goals beat do-your-best or no assigned goals at a pooled d = 0.66.

Recognise that assigned goals carry normative information about expected performance and so shape self-efficacy and confidence, which in turn determines how difficult a goal the student will next choose (self-efficacy to attainment d = 0.46 to 0.92).

Explain why difficult goals work — they give a clearer notion of success and direct attention to relevant behaviours, whereas do-your-best goals are easily attained since almost anything can be defined as one's best.

Pair goals with feedback: goals tell students what level of performance to attain so they can direct and evaluate effort, and feedback lets them track performance against the goal and adjust effort, direction or strategy.

Treat commitment as helpful but not necessary for goal attainment, except for special education students where it is decisive, and expect the commitment-performance link (0.36 to 0.47) to strengthen as goal difficulty rises.
Set drill tasks at 90 per cent or more known to unknown items (d = 1.19) and never below 50 per cent known (0.49), with the ratio nearer 95 per cent known words for learning to read.

Apply the known-to-unknown ratio principally in the acquisition stage (d = 1.09) rather than the proficiency stage (0.39), and flag that no evidence exists for the maintenance, generalization or application stage.
Have the teacher rather than the student choose tasks at the known-to-unknown ratio, since teacher-chosen ratios produce much greater effects.
Note the matching premise fails at its first step: teachers identify their students' learning preferences correctly only 30 per cent of the time against a chance rate of 25 per cent.

Expect advance organizers to have only a small facilitative effect that increases over time (0.21), with written organizers weaker than non-written and no effect at all for low-ability or low-knowledge learners.
Diagnose why organizers and objectives underperform: they too often stay specific, ignore challenge, and carry no notion of what would count as success in attaining the objective.
Use concept mapping only once students already hold the surface knowledge of the concept to be mapped, since it cannot substitute for initial content teaching.

Attribute the concept-mapping gain to the heuristic process of organizing and synthesizing, not the map format: it barely beats asking students to construct an outline (0.19) but substantially beats lectures or discussion (0.74).
Have students construct concept maps (0.81) rather than study prepared ones (0.37), with the strongest effects when students supply the terms regardless of who then draws the map.
Use problem-based learning only after students already hold the surface knowledge, since it has limited and even negative effects on surface knowledge but positive effects on deeper learning.
Target concept mapping at lower-ability students who lack organizing and synthesizing skills, where effects are highest, rather than at higher-ability or highly verbal students.
Target problem-based learning at application (0.40) and principles (0.75) rather than concepts (-0.04), since the application of knowledge, not its development, is the heart of its success.
Do not build instruction on learning hierarchies: overall effects are very low (0.19 on learning, 0.09 on time saved) and they work at elementary level (0.44) but not high school (0.07).
Treat a learning intention without success criteria as incomplete: students may know what is to be learnt yet not know how their performance will be judged or when they have succeeded.
Treat a learning intention as a discrepancy-creating process — a deliberate gap between present performance and target — that both teacher and student must be able to locate, size and plan to reduce.

Diagnose why good intentions fall short: decisions are inappropriately compared, inadequately evaluated against alternatives, aimed at structural and working conditions rather than teaching strategies, and evaluated by models that seek success and ignore failure.

Recognise the failure mode: the outcome of Project Follow Through was more resources for the methods that did not work, because the romantic view of students discovering learning outweighed a method requiring attention to detail and teaching specific skills.
Budget for the time cost of mastery testing: it benefits lower-ability students most (0.96 against 0.52 overall) but increases required instructional time by about 25 per cent.

Expect mastery programmes to raise examination performance by about half a standard deviation, especially for low-aptitude students, while increasing time on instructional tasks — and note self-paced versions often reduce college completion rates.

Read the null mastery-learning finding as an artefact of its inclusion rule: barring feedback-corrective cycles left only seven articles from a large candidate pool, so it reflects the criteria, not the intervention.

Do not agonize over worked-example format: the overall effect is d = 0.52 with little variation (conventional 0.49, fading 0.60, self-explanation 0.57), so using them at all matters much more than which variant.
Distinguish worked examples for students from exemplars for teachers: the latter have no evidence base, with 50-plus organizations producing them and none able to supply evidence of their effects.

State what the evidence does not require: additional structural resources, particular class sizes, particular students, particular subjects, or particular schools, since effective teaching works similarly for all students, ethnicities and subjects.
Name the mechanism of reward harm: it is a controlling strategy that undermines students taking responsibility for regulating themselves and invites greater surveillance, evaluation and competition.

Report the reward controversy honestly: a competing synthesis found no significant effect on intrinsic motivation with verbal rewards positive and tangible negative, but all these effects are so small that concluding rewards are or are not critical is moot.
Treat feedback as capable of harm: across 470 effect sizes the average is d = 0.38 and 32 per cent of effects are negative, so a feedback intervention can make performance worse.
Work the four feedback levels distinctly — task or product, process used to complete it, self-regulation, and the self as person — since each has different effects.
Use direction as the discriminator of feedback effectiveness: whether it is aimed at task, process or regulation rather than at the self.

Distinguish their functions: feedback tells people what is and goals tell them what is desirable; feedback involves information and goals involve evaluation, and together they are the joint effect of motivation and cognition controlling action.
Pitch feedback at, or just above, the level where the student is currently working, with the standing exception that feedback at the self or personal level is rarely effective.
Avoid self-directed feedback because it makes students avoid the risk of challenging assignments, minimize effort, and develop a high fear of failure in order to protect the self.
Position feedback as what happens second — one powerful answer rather than the answer, occurring too rarely, and sometimes less effective than instruction.
Consider that the frequent-testing gain may come not from frequency but from the tests making learning intentions and success criteria more specific and transparent.
Attribute the testing gain to learning from testing rather than to testing itself: frequent testing gives d = 0.41, rising to 0.62 with feedback and falling to 0.30 without.
Use multiple-try feedback for higher-order outcomes (d = 0.10) but not surface ones (-0.22), since it forces more thought about the question unless the learner guesses randomly out of frustration.
Allow a new assessment form time to work, since performance assessment becomes more effective the longer it has been in place as students and teachers grow adept at it.
Reject lengthening the school day or year: increasing allocated time without increasing productive time is unlikely to improve performance.
Refuse to credit an accountability policy with gains that followed the same trajectories as the years before the policy was enacted.

Reject a single pooled figure for high-stakes testing: effects vary from d = -0.67 to 1.24 and do not depend on whether accountability targets schools, students or both, so the average conceals the disagreement.
Treat coaching as practically unimportant (about d = 0.25 overall, 0.15 on the SAT) from matched or randomized studies, and note that uncontrolled studies report higher and more variable effects.
Where coaching is used, run it five weeks or longer, expecting higher effects for upper-grade students and students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds.

Read retest gains as practice artefacts: much larger with coaching (0.70) than without (0.24), larger on identical tests (0.46) than alternate forms (0.24), and shrinking sharply by a third administration.
Where coaching is justified at all, use practice plus instruction on answering particular items rather than practice on complete examinations or general test-taking instruction.

Account for examiner familiarity, which raises test performance by d = 0.35 — strongest for low socioeconomic status students, on difficult tests, and with longer acquaintance — so an unfamiliar examiner systematically disadvantages some students.
Match question level to intended outcome depth, since question type is the major moderator: surface questions build surface knowing and higher-order questions build deeper understanding.
Tie factual pre-questions to the material being learnt, since unrelated ones turn negative, while higher-order questions facilitate both directly related and unrelated material.
Reject an all-higher-order questioning policy: lower-level questions serve surface information best while a mixture of lower and higher-level questions serves deeper understanding.
Monitor implementation, a powerful moderator: studies that monitored showed positive effects (0.66) while those without monitoring showed negative effects (-0.10).
Structure class sessions to elicit, teach and listen to students questioning each other, since analyzing the questions students ask may matter more than teacher questioning.

Run reciprocal teaching properly: students take turns as teacher using summarizing, questioning, clarifying and predicting, supported by teacher-student dialogue over a text, so they monitor their own understanding.
Test understanding through student-to-student dialogue rather than teacher questioning, since a teacher can leave a lesson confident of high-quality teaching and be wrong.

Treat teacher immediacy as an affective lever (d = 1.15) rather than a cognitive one (0.16), with its proposed route to cognition running through the affective outcome and functioning as feedback about the teacher's interest and involvement.

Require cognitive and affective empathy from teachers — hearing the intent and emotion behind what a student says and reflecting it back by paraphrasing — and attention to how children define, describe and interpret problems from their own perspective.
Treat time on task as a weak lever (engaged instructional time d = 0.34, reading practice 0.10) compared with what is done in that time.

Give the learner rather than the teacher or system control of pacing, time allocation for mastery, sequencing, choice of practice items and reviewing (learner-controlled 0.41 against system-controlled -0.02).

Distinguish deliberate practice from drill and practice, which is typically dull and repetitive, gives minimal feedback, lacks contextual variability for transfer, and stays at surface knowledge divorced from deeper understanding.
Recognise deliberate practice as the common denominator across direct instruction, peer tutoring, mastery learning and feedback, raising fluency as well as mastery.
Treat drill as a euphemism for practice — repeated learning until mastery — and the key ingredient in mastery learning and deliberate practice, so students do need much of it.
Make deliberate practice engaging: the drill attributes producing the highest effects are learner control, not losing sight of the learning goal, and immediate announcement of correctness.
Embed deliberate practice in a higher-order set of learnings, since practice unrelated to more challenging goals is dull, repetitive and counter to engagement.
Do not infer expertise, knowledge, or skill from cortical thickness or a training-related imaging difference without ruling out time, effort, strategy, motivation, physiology, and predisposition.
Plan three to four exposures to material spread over several days before expecting a reasonable probability that students will learn it.
Space practice rather than mass it (d = 0.46), which improves both acquisition (0.45) and retention (0.51).
Treat tutoring as instruction for the tutor as much as service to the tutee, since tutors gain about as much as those they tutor (0.58 against 0.63).
Treat as untested the conjecture that peer tutoring matters most for new surface-level information while tutors need deeper understanding to teach effectively.

Let students with disabilities tutor: peer tutoring effects do not differ by whether disabled or non-disabled students act as tutors, and special-needs students tutoring other special-needs students gain as much as those they tutor.
Run peer-mediated interventions for disabled students in general classes (d = 0.56) rather than special classes (0.32).

Note that mentoring outcomes are unrelated to frequency of contact or relationship length, and are higher for trained than untrained mentors and for academic rather than at-risk or workplace mentoring.
Take self-monitoring the further step to self-evaluation: ticking off completed tasks gives d = 0.45 while judging what was monitored against a standard gives 0.62.

Deprioritise the passive self-regulation strategies — environmental restructuring (0.22), time management and imagery (0.44 each), record keeping — which involve no active engagement with the content.
Do not read an early dip as failure: achievement can fall immediately after a study-skills intervention is introduced before it works.
Do not generalize a study-skill benefit across ability groups: note taking facilitates test performance for less skilled learners but not for highly skilled ones.

Use mnemonic methods with special needs students, where they produce the highest effects of all, while noting that study-skills programmes for students struggling at college level produce quite low effects.
Bound the teaching-strategies finding: it ranks among the highest influences (d = 0.60) but most of those meta-analyses concern special education or students with learning difficulties.
For students with identified learning disabilities use sequencing, drill repetition and strategy cues, strongest in creativity (0.84), reading comprehension (0.82) and vocabulary (0.79).

Use scaffolding of task difficulty, directed response and Socratic questioning, step-by-step sequencing prompts, drill-repetition-practice-review, segmentation and strategy cueing as the highest-impact strategies for learning-disabled students.
Prioritise reviewing notes (d = 0.45) over taking them, and give students the instructor's notes as an exemplar and rubric (0.82).
Prefer instructional techniques designed for the student (d = 0.73) over those designed for the teacher (0.61).
Expect study-skills effects to fall as the outcome gets deeper — memory d = 1.09, reproductive performance 0.69, transformational performance 0.53.

Target self-questioning and self-verbalization at learners in early or intermediate skill acquisition and of lower to middle ability, since higher-ability students already use a range of self-regulation strategies.
Develop self-regulation by giving learners meaningful goals, capacity-matched challenges, targeted feedback, metacognitive prompts, and responsibility for monitoring and adapting progress.
Teach self-regulation explicitly through bounded autonomy, meaningful responsibility, interest-aware tasks, goal setting, method selection, monitoring, and adjustment.
Preserve learner agency within sufficient guidance, and distinguish metacognitive monitoring from control when teaching self-regulation.
Keep self-regulation intervention claims tied to trained skills, and test transfer and cultural applicability before asserting a general domain-independent capacity.
Expect technology-based self-regulation and deep-questioning skills to require many examples and hours, and adapt support to the learner rather than relying on one brief script.
Study self-regulation against specific goals, disciplines, environments, instruction, and developmental periods, and test durability and transfer rather than presuming a context-free skill.
Place self-questioning before (d = 0.94) or after (0.86) a lesson rather than interspersed during it (0.52), delay rather than make it immediate (0.72 against 0.54), and model it (0.69 against 0.47).

Note that instructionally irrelevant choices such as pen colour or background music outperform relevant ones because they cost little effort and carry no learning consequence, and that too many choices overwhelm.
Do not use any aptitude-treatment interaction as a direct guide to instruction: none is well enough confirmed, a conclusion reached after comprehensive review and repeatedly reconfirmed.
Do not compare an aptitude-treatment interaction effect with the main-effect influences, since it is computed after main effects are removed.
Treat learning-styles inventories as non-predictive: diverger, assimilator, converger and accommodator all fall at d = 0.28 to 0.29, so no style predicts achievement better than any other.

Exclude the largest pro-learning-styles syntheses: they rest mainly on dissertations supervised by the authors, use attitudinal outcomes and tiny samples, and in at least one case mistook a multiple R from a regression for the treatment effect size.

Cite the field-level verdict on learning styles: few studies meet minimum acceptability criteria, with overstatement, poor items and assessments, low validity, negligible impact on practice, and advocacy aimed at commercial ends.
Watch for selective reporting of one significant test from many run, as when only a third-grade matched-versus-control comparison was interpreted and entered into a synthesis.

Extract the working features from individualization and deliver them in groups: adapt instruction to assessed needs, let students progress at their own pace, use periodic evaluation to inform mastery, and have students assist one another.

Include the instructional components that work for learning-disabled students: sequencing, drill-repetition-practice, segmenting information for later synthesis, controlling task difficulty through prompts and cues, using technology, systematically modeling problem-solving steps, and small interactive groups.

Read the personal nature of learning as requiring awareness of each student's progression, how they learn alone, with others and with adults, and what they bring from home and culture — not as requiring individualized instruction.
Welcome rather than merely tolerate errors, alongside learning intentions, success criteria, attention to task challenge, and feedback that reduces the gap.
Combine direct and strategy instruction rather than choosing between them, since models including both produce higher effects than either alone.

Combine direct instruction with strategy instruction to remediate learning disabilities, since the two approaches are somewhat independent and both are needed to maximize the effect (0.84 combined against 0.72 for either alone).

Attribute a divergent synthesis to its method before its subject: one reporting far lower teaching effects drew on European studies rarely included elsewhere, admitted only studies controlling for student prerequisites, and used a different teaching model.

Prioritise domain-specific processing, the one teaching dimension that consistently stands out (d = 0.43 overall, 0.45 on cognitive outcomes) against near-zero effects for time for learning, organization, social context, goal orientation, evaluation and regulation.

Prioritise the highest-leverage instructional moves across 4,000 effect sizes: matching (1.32), experimental inquiry (1.14), cues (1.13), note taking (0.99), goal specification (0.97) and questions (0.93), with information generalization lowest (0.11).
Adopt reciprocal teaching without specialist delivery: it produces d = 0.74 and ordinary classroom teachers achieve the same effect as the study authors.
Note reciprocal teaching results do not vary by grade level, number of sessions, group size, number of strategies taught, or who did the training, so implementation choices there are free.
Check the assessment before comparing reciprocal-teaching results: effects are far larger on experimenter-developed comprehension assessments (0.88) than on standardized tests (0.32).

Distinguish Direct Instruction as a defined method from didactic teacher-led talking, since the mantra that constructivism is good and direct instruction bad is contradicted by the meta-analytic results.

Refute the claim that Direct Instruction suits only low-level skills and weaker or younger students: effects are similar for regular (0.99) and special education or lower ability (0.86) students, for word attack (0.64) and high-level comprehension (0.54), and across phases.
Combine input, modeling of the expected end product with critical aspects labelled and compared to exemplars, and checking for understanding before practice begins.

Decontextualize independent practice across enough different contexts that the skill applies beyond where it was learnt — inference practised on dinosaurs then on whales — since failure to do this is held responsible for most student failure to transfer.
Note that Direct Instruction effects are not merely teacher effects, since mathematics lessons delivered by videodisc produced effects close to d = 1.00.

Note that implementation fidelity did not rescue a video-game-based multimedia curriculum, which produced very low effects in mathematics (0.13) and language arts (0.18) in both high and low quality implementations.
Note that the typical teacher effect is about d = 0.15 to 0.35 and that effects rise markedly beyond that only when there is an intervention or innovation.

Distinguish problem-solving teaching (0.61) from problem-based learning (0.15, rank 118), and prefer cooperative arrangements over individualistic (0.59) and competitive (0.54) ones while noting competitive versus individualistic is weak (0.24).

Train teachers in heuristic methods — understanding the problem, planning, carrying out the plan, examining the solution — since that is the teacher characteristic with the most positive effect on problem-solving performance (d = 0.71), and support problems with diagrams, figures or sketches.

Define problem-based learning by its six characteristics — student-centered learning, small groups, a tutor as facilitator, authentic problems presented first, problems used as tools to reach the required knowledge, and self-directed acquisition of new information — before evaluating it.
Note problem-based learning moves self-directed learning (0.54) and attitude toward learning (0.52) more than problem solving itself (0.30).
Use cooperative or competitive arrangements over individualistic ones, since both outperform individualistic methods and that points again to the power of peers in the learning equation.
Teach a repertoire of problem-solving strategies and interleave decisions about which strategy is appropriate and efficient.

Rank the technology and out-of-school approaches: interactive video (0.52) leads while distance education (0.09), home-school programs (0.16), web-based learning (0.18) and co-teaching (0.19) are near the bottom.

Note web-delivered K-12 distance programmes match traditional classrooms (0.15) with no moderation by content, grade, school type, frequency, pacing, timing, instructor preparation or student setting.
Judge adjunct aids by how and where they are used in the text and the sophistication of the student using them, not by their presence.
Use animation only when representational and central to the concept being learnt (d = 0.89), not decoratively (0.29); realism level makes no difference.

Do not choose between inductive and deductive sequencing on evidence: whether examples precede or follow generalizations makes no difference across knowledge, application, process, transfer, comprehension and problem solving.
Teach inductive reasoning — detecting generalizations, rules and regularities — which is effective (d = 0.59), and note that making comparisons and contrasts can be taught across contexts.
Treat evidence as providing hypotheses for intelligent problem solving and for inquiring into the ends of education, not rules for action.
Evaluate an inquiry programme on the outcome it actually shifts: it moves science process far more than science content (0.52 against 0.16, or 0.40 against 0.26).
Expect inquiry effects to be greatest at elementary level and to decrease as students progress, and to be higher in biology and physics than chemistry.
Train teachers in inquiry methods as a condition on the effect, since students of teachers who received in-service training significantly outperformed those in traditional programmes.

Consider that inquiry-based instruction may be most powerful where students can think critically but have not previously been encouraged to, since the four largest effects came from atypical populations whose thinking had not been valued.

Report the problem-based learning trade-off: a strong negative effect on knowledge (-0.78) alongside a positive effect on skills (0.66), leaving students with less knowledge but better recall of what they have because it is more elaborated.
Treat working conditions as small but positive, meaning they should not be made worse even though improving them is not the lever on learning.

Do not frame cooperation and competition as mutually exclusive: a system can rank top internationally on both, and the usual research framing of one against the other misses that both may be beneficial.
Judge a method by whether it produces greater outcomes and deeper comprehension rather than by whether students enjoy it, since preference is not the criterion for adoption.
Reject student preference as a basis for choosing an instructional method, since students preferred less guided methods yet learned less from them.
Use cooperation with intergroup competition, which outperforms interpersonal competition and individualistic effort and is particularly effective with tangible rewards and maximizing tasks.
Do not use cooperative structures for rote decoding and correcting tasks, where cooperation gives no advantage.
Use cooperative experiences to build relationships between individuals from different ethnic backgrounds and between handicapped and non-handicapped individuals.

Distinguish the three arrangements precisely: competition can be against other students, one's own previous performance or a curriculum standard, whereas in an individualistic situation others' outcomes are simply irrelevant.

Expect an imposed whole-school reform to produce real gains that do not survive the sponsor: even below-average teachers improved and state scores rose, but the schools reverted once the sponsoring superintendent left.
Expect lower effects when an intervention is delivered as part of a comprehensive top-down reform, because teachers then do not evaluate whether it is working for them.
Recognise the classroom game in which some students retell the story and nod at the right times, and hold that learning occurs when the students learn, not when the teacher has satisfactorily taught.
Recognise that teachers know very little about what is going on in their classrooms, which is why learning outcomes feel unpredictable, mysterious and uncontrollable to them.

Discount developer-run evaluations: effect sizes from comprehensive reform studies run by the programmes' own developers are systematically higher, and about half the programmes are still evaluated only by their developers.

Allow about five years before judging a comprehensive school reform, since effects become most apparent only after the fifth year of implementation and do not vary by socioeconomic resources or subject.

For adolescents with learning disabilities use extended deliberate practice, expecting the strongest gains in meta-cognition and understanding text and the hardest area to change to be learned attributions such as self-efficacy and effort.
Fund academic skills (d = 0.28) and guidance sessions (0.41) for high-risk college students rather than remedial programmes, which show zero effect (0.05).
Prefer anxiety reduction (0.22 to 0.56) and concentration and engagement (0.48 to 1.09) to resilience programmes for at-risk students, which show essentially nothing (0.03).
Plan for institutional decay: special programme effects are stronger when new and weaker once institutionalized, so colleges are better at starting programmes than at sustaining them.
Treat co-teaching and team teaching as unevidenced rather than disproved: the literature supports neither its critics nor its advocates, and the measured effects are low (0.06 to 0.31).

Apply the principles rather than adopt the methods, since a low-effect method such as team teaching (0.19) could produce much greater effects if run with attention to student-teacher feedback and challenging goals.

Report computer-assisted instruction at d = 0.37 across 76 meta-analyses, a positive difference 25 times in a hundred, and note effects do not correlate with year of study (r = 0.05), which refutes the claim that benefit grows with the sophistication of the technology.
Note computer effects do not differ by grade, ability level or intervention duration, and differ across subjects in no meaningful pattern.
State that computers can increase the probability of learning but there is no necessary relation between having computers, using computers, and learning outcomes.

Recognise that most computer studies compare classes taught with and without computers rather than students learning in different ways with computers, so the literature answers a weaker question than the one usually asked of it.

Expect teachers to use computers for personal and administrative purposes while struggling to relate them to their conception of teaching, since computer use is not part of their grammar of schooling.
Provide more than ten hours of computer pre-training or none at all: under ten hours is not merely unproductive but counterproductive, while over ten yields up to 72 per cent additional gain.
Concentrate computer training into a few weeks rather than spreading it: effects fall from d = 0.67 for courses under 4 weeks to 0.32 for courses over 14 weeks.

Choose the computer use by effect: structured tutorials greatest (0.71), then programming (0.50) and word processing (0.42), with drill and practice (0.34), simulations (0.34) and problem solving (0.26) lower.

Learn from computer games that repetitive drill with increasing challenge can be motivating, and from the finding that computer drill routines frequently beat traditional teaching, which should prompt teachers to ask why.

Use word processors for writing, since students write more and better — especially weaker writers — make more revisions and fewer errors, and length and quality are highly positively related so the extra output is not padding (d = 0.40).

Put students at computers in pairs (0.54 to 0.96) rather than alone (0.25 to 0.56) or in larger groups (0.39), since large groups reduce each student's opportunity to explore beliefs and let dominant members crowd out submissive ones.

Expect paired computer work to raise positive peer interaction (0.33), use of task strategies (0.50) and perseverance (0.48), while students working alone request more teacher help (0.67) and finish faster.
Form heterogeneous computer groups (d = 1.15) rather than homogeneous ones (0.51), though both beat working alone.

Match the social structure to the software: pairs for system-controlled close-ended tutorial or practice programs, and discussion-focused arrangements for exploratory programs and general-purpose tools so each member articulates and explains alternative hypotheses.
Build computer feedback as explanations (0.66) and remediation (0.73) rather than simply providing the correct answer (-0.11).

Make computer tasks genuinely challenging: effects are positive for challenging tasks (0.13) but negative for moderately challenging (-0.34) and non-challenging ones (-0.57), so there is no point running computer activities without challenge.
Expect the seven principles of good online-learning practice to yield very small effects (0.07 to 0.14), highest for encouraging student-faculty contact and lowest for emphasizing time on task.

Treat web-based learning as weak (d = 0.18 to 0.24 with huge variability, generally below other computer-based interventions) partly because it often ignores instructional design fundamentals such as interaction and timely feedback.

Use visualization in interactive video (0.71) to convey the essence of the message, preferring illustrated materials to verbal descriptions especially with high school students, and colour to black and white.
Give students both visual and verbal materials, because verbal material alone leaves an impoverished visual mental model insufficient to integrate with the verbal one.

Deploy hypermedia as a supplement rather than a substitute, with regular class teachers rather than specialists, and in elementary rather than high school, where it beats traditional instruction most.

Treat resources such as adjunct aids and computers as adding value only once teachers have learned to optimize their use — by diversifying teaching strategies, providing alternative practice, and increasing feedback to learner and teacher.
Keep simulations short — up to one week is more effective than longer — while noting the ability and grade-level findings conflict across syntheses.
Use science simulations confirmatively for surface outcomes (0.44 against 0.27 for free exploration), noting the two approaches do not differ for deeper thinking outcomes.
Note that simulation effects are far greater in colleges (0.49) than K-12 (0.14) and show no effect on attitudes or on retention two weeks later.

Reject programmed instruction, which consistently ranks near the bottom of method comparisons — below tutoring, computer-assisted instruction, Keller's system and audio-tutorials — with no support for students enjoying it.
Attribute the one respectable programmed-instruction result (0.40) to its use of older, more self-regulating students rather than to the method.

State the distance education finding precisely: no difference in outcomes between distance and face-to-face students, which is not the same as distance education not working — the medium is not the message.
Expect that once the technology of a distance programme is working and paid for, the remaining difference in outcomes is attributable to the quality of the teaching.
Expect zero achievement effect from both synchronous (-0.10 to -0.02) and asynchronous (0.05 to 0.06) distance education, with negative to zero effects on attitude and retention.
Design distance programmes around student interaction with peers and instructors, the differentiating quality that explains why post-1998 studies with interaction facilities differ from earlier ones.
Judge distance and blended learning by instructional design and interaction quality, not delivery mode; add in-person or study support when learners lack needed self-regulation.
Explain why deep-learning homework fails: it needs the teaching cycle of learning, feedback and monitoring, whereas rehearsal of surface knowledge can proceed with minimal supervision.
Expose the lens behind evidence-based claims: what counts as evidence, what is excluded, and how it is marshalled into a story are decisions the phrase conceals.
Do not read causation into an effect size: the term implies it but the causal claim is often not defensible, and providing explanation is the harder and more valuable task.

Read an effect size with four checks: the variability around it, the unexplained variance that limits the importance of the explained, the reference point used, and interactions with other variables that can dramatically alter the conclusion.
Frame synthesis as abduction — inferences to the best explanation — and hold the resulting story to be bold enough to be potentially disprovable.

Cite the voucher evidence: over a decade the disparity between top and bottom schools increased dramatically, with parents fleeing schools with high minority proportions rather than moving toward higher measured outcomes, which were not even published.
Note that children from more advantaged families were the major beneficiaries of the voucher system and its loudest advocates, so school choice redistributed rather than raised quality.
Ask what effort a task elicits rather than what interest it provokes, since it is the effort, not the interest level, that matters.
Set the progress benchmark per implementation or year at d = 0.40 for every student, at least 0.30, and certainly not less than 0.20.

Note that schools which later proved academically improving reported higher trust than non-improving ones (0.61 reading, 0.64 mathematics), and that trust maximizes the occurrence of error so feedback can be powerful.

Account for the three worlds of a classroom — the public world of teacher-led discussion and tasks, the private-social world of peer whispers and notes, and the private-individual world of self-talk — each with its own patterns, rules and discourse.

Treat classroom observation as missing up to 40 per cent of what occurs among students, which is why individual audio monitoring was needed and why critical reflection by teachers is barely adequate as a data source.

Account for what the class already knows and for private learning: students already know at least 40 per cent of what teachers intend them to learn, a third of what each student learns is learned by no other student, and a quarter of concepts learned depend on private peer talk or self-designed activity.

Separate the criteria for successful learning from those for successful classroom management, which in most teachers' minds are the same, so enthusiasm, puzzlement and questions are read as evidence that teaching is going well.
Put the desirable lens of success in place by having teachers seek evidence that their teaching may not have been successful, because we otherwise see evidence of our success everywhere.

Seek disconfirmation at every level: teaching may fail for some students, for parts of the learning intentions, or against aspects of the success criteria, and the goals, challenge level and engagement processes all need constant questioning.

Recognise that teachers measure success by the satisfaction of doing a good job and the approval of parents and principals rather than by student outcomes, because the incentive structure does not emphasize student performance.
Notice that neither teachers nor students talk about learning: teachers talk about resources, how long an activity should take, and what happens if it is unfinished.

Use the activator list — reciprocal teaching (0.74), feedback (0.72), self-verbalization and meta-cognition (0.67), Direct Instruction (0.59), mastery learning (0.57) — over the facilitator list of simulations (0.32), inquiry teaching (0.31), smaller classes (0.21), problem-based learning (0.15) and whole language (0.06).

Note that ranks 11 to 30 are dominated by teacher and teaching influences, from teacher-student relationships (0.72) and spaced practice (0.71) through meta-cognitive strategies (0.69) to mastery learning (0.58) and worked examples (0.57).

Note that almost all state and federal policy addresses structural issues — resources, class size, choice, curriculum, tests and high-stakes assessment — and it is rare to find a policy that relates to teaching.

Heed the prescription trap: a prescribed teaching package works mainly where teachers are poorly prepared and there is a history of failure and disorder, is hard to maintain, and may leave students dependent when they meet new tasks.

Watch the consequences of transmission teaching: teachers seek more engaging rather than more challenging tasks, more frontal talk and questions they already know the answers to, and students come to believe progress depends on teacher-directed methods.

Treat as speculative the suggestion that what matters more is the teacher's conception of progress in the subject, knowledge of when to intervene, knowledge of learning theory, and openness to alternative ways to teach the content.

Recognise that it is far easier to discuss and fund working conditions — class size, salary, buildings, longer days — or parent appeasements such as computers, school choice and more examinations, than to change the transmission model of teaching.
Replace the barren question what works? with what works best, compared to what alternatives, when, for whom, and to what ends.

Note that any recommendation about what works best invokes cultural claims, since classrooms enact individualism, community or collectivism and those values drive interaction and discourse patterns — with mistakes treated as embarrassing in some cultures and put in the public domain in others.

Expect mathematics lessons to look consistent across countries: students solve problems alone or in whole-class groups rather than small peer groups, textbooks and worksheets are used extensively, and teachers talk eight times more than students.
Note that differential effects by school subject were hard to find, since good teaching and the most powerful influences seem similar across domains, which undercuts subject chauvinism.
Report that there was no preponderance of evidence supporting the importance of subject knowledge or pedagogical content knowledge for student outcomes.

Bound the corpus's reach: most tests used measure surface features effectively, deep learning somewhat, and constructed representations rarely, so the results speak more to surface and deep knowing than to conceptual understanding.
Treat knowing at the constructed level as an activity rather than a thing — reciprocally constructed in the individual-environment-teacher interaction and not easily captured by a one-off test.
Cast progress in terms of increasingly challenging demands from the underlying concepts and the proficiencies test scores supposedly measure, not in terms of activities, events or scores.
Reject the weakest evidence claims: that this year beat last year, that no one complained, or that weaker students reflect what they brought to class.

Define going backwards broadly: not only students who fall behind their starting point but those who miss the expected yearly gain and those who fall short of what they could achieve because their teachers hold low expectations.

Take the scale of regression seriously: in some schools 80 per cent of students went backwards in a year, notably in grade 9 mathematics where students first meet algebra, disengage, form beliefs about their low performance and often drop the subject.

Ask teachers what percentage of their students go backwards in a year with them, since the question is rarely considered and its absence reduces the chance of finding those students before the problems compound.
Explain the consequences of a zero reference point: it is why it is hard to find a below-average teacher, why every teacher is considered effective, and why all can claim to have added value.

Note the ordering of critical change agents in therapy: knowledge and skills, a plan of action, strategies to overcome setbacks, a high sense of confidence, monitoring progress, commitment to achieve, social and environmental support, and last, freedom, control or choice.
Expect an innovation to change during implementation, so what is evaluated at the end is not what was initiated.
Target the reasons for non-change rather than the mechanics of change, since the key issue is less how to change than why we do not.

Name the psychological processes sustaining current practice: the need for certainty, control and simplicity, seeking confirming examples, failing to seek evidence of what is not working, attributing failure to the student but success to the teacher, and immunity to different ideas.

Expect revolutionary ideas to be resisted because every successful teacher has a vested intellectual, social and financial interest in the status quo — and note that welcoming every new idea would produce chaos.

Locate resistance in the conceptions of teaching and learning shared by teachers, expressed as leave me alone to teach my way, rather than in a general resistance to change — schools are constantly changing.
Account for teaching happening largely out of sight and hearing of other teachers, which is why teachers rely on war stories and personal experience to construct shared understanding.
Prefer statistical to clinical or intuitive judgment, which it beats across 173 effect sizes spanning 56 years, replicating a finding first established in the 1950s.

Expect that finding to be ignored, because practitioners lack familiarity with statistical methods, value interpersonal cues, believe statistics dehumanize, and recall their correct predictions but not their wrong ones.

Confront the attribution pattern: of more than 5,000 children referred to school psychologists for failing, not one referral located the problem in a poor instructional programme, poor school practice or a poor teacher.

Challenge a system that concludes all problems are caused by defects in the children and none by defects in the system, and demand to know where the practice produced effective results and where the data show superiority over successful programmes rather than over the last failed attempt.
Ask of any innovation where it was installed with effective results, where teachers were trained to perform uniformly within its guidelines, and which historically successful teachers endorse it.

Note the inverse relation: the closer an innovation gets to the core of schooling the less likely it is to influence teaching and learning at scale, while those furthest from teaching and learning are most likely to become national policy.

Note that vast sums are invested in educational innovations, changes and policies without much evidence that the investment moves student outcomes, though it may improve teachers' and students' working conditions.

Rely on professional development rather than legislation, since it is nearly impossible to legislate changes to conceptions of teaching and learning and most policy changes therefore have little or no effect — policy churn agitates the surface while life below goes on uninterrupted.
Abandon accountability, government pressure, compulsion and the stick as instruments of conception change, since they rarely change the conceptions or lens of teachers.

Treat education as never neutral because its fundamental purpose is intervention or behaviour change, which makes teaching a moral profession facing questions such as why teach this rather than that and how to teach in defensible ways.

Hold that teaching involves ethics in its aims, methods and relationships and requires respect for autonomy and for reason, so talk of the technicist, competent or skilled teacher should remind us that education is essentially a moral enterprise.
Pose the key question as whether teaching can shift from an immature to a mature profession — from opinions to evidence, from subjective judgment and personal contact to critique of judgments.
Disclose that only meta-analyses were given the privilege of inclusion, and that a review of non-meta-analytic and qualitative studies could yield a richer and more nuanced statement of the evidence.

Count the most critical costs: opportunity costs where students lose access to activities that truly make a difference and which their peers are benefiting from, and the suffering costs of exposure to the least effective interventions.
Count the effort costs of the reforms with most power over learning — those of teachers, school leaders and students — which are too often assumed free or taken from teachers' social and home life.
Refuse familiarity, enjoyment and anecdotal support as offsets to the suffering cost of a low-effectiveness intervention.
Do not expect increasing the share of spending on instruction to affect learning by itself, since 60 per cent already goes there.

Plan against the two-century base rate: about 85 per cent of teachers resist changing what they believe works, ten per cent will change to be more efficient, and five per cent will try new innovations.
Expect diminishing marginal returns: doubling learning time does not double outcomes, and adding more influences and methods can lead to fewer outcomes than choosing the optimal smaller set.
Seek the right combination of interventions in the right proportions to produce an interaction effect, rather than accumulating individually effective methods.

Treat adoption as a process rather than a discrete event, moving through awareness, knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation and confirmation, with imprecise boundaries and not all phases occurring.

Plan diffusion in stages: it starts with a few teachers who are open to change, more educated, self-confident and less concerned with others' norms, spreads once a critical mass forms, and reaches the final fifth only with difficulty.

Hold agencies, departments and teacher educators to the standard they demand of teachers, since they are reluctant to accept evidence contrary to current policy and prefer changes to structural and working conditions.

Define damage broadly: not only teachers with zero or negative gains, but teachers and schools that do not aim for and reach the d = 0.40 hinge-point, condemning their students to mediocrity and lesser opportunities.

Cite Project Follow Through at full scale: over 72,000 students across more than 180 sites over ten years, where all but one programme had close to zero or negative effects and only Direct Instruction produced positive effects on basic skills, deeper comprehension, social and affective measures.
Note the long-run result: Direct Instruction students followed to the end of schooling were twice as likely to graduate high school and scored higher in reading (0.43) and mathematics (0.28).
Name the rejection of an evidenced method in favour of an ideologically preferred one as the mark of an immature profession lacking a solid scientific base and respecting opinion over evidence.

Draw the medical parallel: medicine was once equally unscientific, with treatments tried on trial and error lasting decades before being abandoned, and evidence-based practice was the mechanism that drove out dogma, since dogma does not destroy itself.

Treat as speculative the suggestion that equity litigation, clinical trials of educational treatments and international outcome standards will be education's analogues of the external pressure that drove medicine's evidence-based revolution.
Ratchet academic demand consistently — slightly more advanced books, slightly longer and more complex writing — rather than holding difficulty constant.
Use the three discriminators that separate experienced experts from experienced non-experts — challenge, deep representation, and monitoring and feedback — out of thirteen candidate dimensions.

Nurture and challenge intellectual and imaginative capacity out to horizons unsullied by self-fulfilling minimalist expectations, rather than patronizing students with lowest-common-denominator content or crushing their love of learning with boring pedagogy.
Teach students with humanity and sensitivity as developing human beings worthy of genuine respect, enlightened discipline and imaginative flair.
Refuse to limit the exploration of evolving knowledge to repetitively recycled worksheets, and ensure legitimate progression of learning from one day, week, month, term and year to the next.
Use the rank-ordered barometer of 138 influences, from self-reported grades (1.44) to student mobility (-0.34), as the comparative frame for judging any proposed intervention.

Expect technology influences to cluster below the hinge-point, with interactive video 44th (0.52) the exception against computer-assisted instruction 71st (0.37), simulations 82nd (0.33), audio-visual methods 104th (0.22), web-based learning 112th (0.18) and distance education 126th (0.09).

Note that the differentiation family performs far worse than its advocacy suggests: matching style of learning 62nd (0.41), aptitude-treatment interactions 108th (0.19) and student control over learning 132nd (0.04).
Use an analogy only with an explicit mapping of relevant similarities and a check for misconceptions the comparison may induce.
Use worked examples to expose why each step works and connect the procedure to its concept, not to induce step copying.
Pair high expectations and constructive criticism with credible care, concrete support, and policies consistent with learners' capacity to improve.
Activate relevant prior knowledge while deliberately surfacing mismatches and counterevidence, because schemas can both support learning and bias attention and recall.
Weight replicated controlled evidence and syntheses most strongly, but use methodological pluralism when necessary and keep each design's inferential limits visible.
Do not generalize narrow samples or laboratory findings directly to broad populations and classrooms; establish population relevance and perform explicit translation.
Recruit diverse populations and measure intersecting cultural, socioeconomic, demographic, and within-group variation before generalizing learning findings broadly.
Translate group-level evidence to an individual by integrating relevant mechanisms, determinants, outcomes, and context while retaining robust population knowledge.
Design school environments with learners and communities by examining cultural fit in language, interaction, time, collaboration, observation, instruction, and demonstrations of competence.
Use joint problem solving and culturally meaningful tools to extend participation beyond current independent capability, recognizing that tools and community practices reshape cognition over time.
Reduce avoidable threat and anxiety while connecting learning to meaningful goals, because worry consumes resources needed for task-focused thought.
Use physical activity as a potential support for cognition, favoring appropriately demanding coordinated activity when relevant, but preserve the evidence's age, task, and outcome limits.

Encourage physical, intellectual, social, and work engagement for healthy aging while distinguishing observational associations from tested causal programs and physically taxing work from beneficial exercise.
Prevent developmental neurotoxin exposure while analyzing learning outcomes within the larger system of physical, social, caregiving, and institutional conditions.

For complex authentic learning, connect verbal, visual, symbolic, procedural, spatial, and applied representations and support collaboration through shared artifacts, distributed work, and exchanged failures.
Communicate descriptive norms carefully: publicize productive peer behavior and avoid warnings that make harmful behavior appear common.

Use models to organize observations, generate plausible explanations, predict new cases, and communicate, while making each model's purpose, assumptions, uncertainty, and boundary conditions explicit.
Let learners construct models with diagrams, simulations, or other representations, but provide enough guidance to keep construction productive.
Protect developmentally sensitive periods with high-quality relationships, language, education, and other necessary inputs, especially for children facing deprivation.
Prevent severe early deprivation and provide high-quality relational, linguistic, and sensory environments as early as possible because substantial recovery is possible but time-sensitive.
Treat the brain as plastic interacting networks shaped by repeated culturally situated experience, not as isolated regions with fixed single functions.
Translate developmental neuroscience cautiously into age-responsive hypotheses, then evaluate them in educational settings across adolescence and later life.
Interpret aging through gradual, nonuniform trajectories and available compensatory resources shaped by prior learning and experience, not chronological age alone.
Structure older-adult training around retained knowledge, reduced time pressure, self-efficacy, cognitive and emotional needs, and immediate relevance.
Evaluate aging by function-specific trajectories and individual context, distinguishing cognitive resources from learning and considering social connection, culture, community, and cohort effects.

Strengthen children's executive control through scaffolded social and self-directed activities involving planning, role switching, checking, symbolic play, and negotiated self-management alongside adult-led instruction.
Match memory support and assessment to the required precision: later-life gist can support integration, but exact source and detail require targeted encoding and consolidation.
Begin with plausible prior beliefs, actively seek diagnostic disconfirming evidence, and revise as decisive evidence accumulates.
Reassess once-useful biases and routines when environments change, because efficient selectivity and automatized methods can impede adaptation.
Design for older learners from their individual cognitive profile and retained domain knowledge, not an average age trend in speeded reasoning.
Support older learners with self-paced links to relevant prior knowledge, while treating unfamiliar-domain difficulty and age trends as hypotheses rather than capacity verdicts.
Evaluate explanations for evidential adequacy, retained detail, exceptions, and interacting causes rather than rewarding a single simple story.
When belonging uncertainty is active, normalize early difficulty as common and temporary without denying real exclusion or barriers.
Generate multiple independent candidate solutions before refinement when early commitment risks fixation.
Interpret goal orientation in cultural context and preserve within-group variation rather than classifying learners or cultures as simply individualistic or collectivistic.
Analyze cultural mindset and self-construal as multidimensional, situational, and ecoculturally grounded; no independent or interdependent perspective is universally superior.

Build school resilience through meaningful autonomy, supportive leadership, collegial staff, coherent behavior support, effective instruction, belonging, and audits of bias in expectations and discipline.
Monitor unequal participation in collaboration, legitimate multiple defensible perspectives, and require negotiation of a shared product without suppressing supported minority interpretations.
Use an aligned assessment system with distinct methods for formative learning, individual certification, and program monitoring rather than forcing one measure to serve every purpose.
Design assessment from an explicit model of competence: define claims, elicit diagnostic observations, and specify how responses support interpretations.

Use research-grounded learning progressions to sequence instruction, model intermediate thinking and misconceptions, build diagnostic items, and identify likely next steps without imposing one invariant path.
For complex-system understanding, let learners construct and manipulate coordinated models, explain correct and incorrect behavior, integrate evidence, and receive misconception-sensitive feedback.
Deploy intelligent tutoring only when tutor form fits the content and learner, authoring cost is sustainable, and curriculum integration and teacher preparation are in place.
Evaluate educational games by the specific content, skill, learner, context, and comparator; neither sustained attention nor game features establish broad cognitive transfer or inherent motivation.
Make young children's technology use developmentally appropriate, high quality, and caregiver-supported, and prevent it from displacing sleep, movement, social interaction, and essential experience.
Use making as guided investigation and revision of how constructed components function, but do not infer makerspace effects from active-learning theory alone.
Align bodily action, physical objects, and digital representations with the concept's spatial or motor structure, and keep embodied-learning claims specific to evaluated systems and outcomes.
Compare embodied virtual, augmented, or sensor-supported learning directly with mental-manipulation alternatives on learning, access, cost, and implementation burden.
Use conversational-agent roles and disagreement to elicit explanation and social reasoning only when confusion is intelligible, relevant, and resolvable.
Treat technology integration as a progression in learner agency and network reach, and prepare educators through sustained collaborative practice aligned with curriculum and learning data.
Embed actionable dashboards in routine curriculum and provide simple interfaces, time, resources, and training; displayed data create value only when users act on valid measures.
Preserve enough user understanding and control to recover when automation fails, unless manual control would itself be unsafe or infeasible.
Design older-adult technology around individual goals, intrinsic benefit, autonomy, prior knowledge, and assessed sensory, memory, distraction, password, motor, and control demands.
Measure digital inclusion as access, skill, support, participation, creation, and advanced opportunity; devices and broadband alone do not close the gap.
Sustain later-life development with attainable growth, use of retained skills, opportunities to help, fair credible feedback, and compensatory social or technological resources.
Map adult learning separately by formality and autonomy so voluntary formal, voluntary informal, required formal, and required informal development remain visible.
Do not infer the cause of an established learning disability from cross-sectional brain differences, because years of altered experience and compensation can also change the brain.
Do not transfer child learning-disability interventions unchanged to adults; use child findings as hypotheses for direct adult evaluation.

Design adult literacy as a supported system for heterogeneous learners that combines cognitive instruction with practical goals, motivation, emotion, relationships, trained instructors, and accessible technology.
Address postsecondary cultural and resource mismatches directly, including time constraints and exclusively independence-oriented norms, rather than interpreting reduced opportunity as low potential.
Tailor workplace training to organizational needs and constraints as well as individual motives, abilities, and prior knowledge.
Evaluate workplace training separately through reaction, immediate knowledge, durable transfer to work behavior, and organizational benefit; no one level is a complete result.
Promote workplace transfer with authentic practice, manageable difficulty, autonomy, peer and supervisor support, clear expectations, and prompt opportunities to use and reinforce new skills.
Teach workplace self-regulation within authentic tasks and the local social system of goals, norms, incentives, resources, and obstacles.
Adapt workplace scaffolding to learner familiarity and task complexity, offering stepwise support for unfamiliar complex work and reducing it as competence grows.
Recognize incidental, peer, trial-and-error, stretch-role, and on-the-job learning as development even when workers experience it as ordinary work.
Foster a learning organization through visible goals, manageable stretch assignments, safe recoverable error, real application, equitable support, and reciprocal employee accountability.
Support continuous career learning by addressing interests, motivation, organizational climate, development opportunities, care, transport, connectivity, time, relationships, and unequal access.
Evaluate autonomous workplace learning through its amount, type, quality, capability change, retention, and perceived learning culture while keeping correlational limits visible.
Research learning through interacting biological, developmental, cognitive, emotional, social, cultural, institutional, and historical systems, joining laboratory and field inquiry across timescales.
Govern longitudinal life-span learning databases through deliberate choices about granularity, coverage, privacy, and use, and retain experiments and qualitative evidence alongside them.
Co-design dashboards and adaptive analytics with training, workflow, governance, and varied-population outcome evaluation; an algorithm or interface is not itself a learning benefit.
Use group categories for bounded population inference without converting them into individual capacity judgments; measure plural cultural systems and socially produced conditions directly.

Use reflexive and methodologically plural research to expose how investigators' cultural assumptions and repeatedly narrow samples shape constructs, questions, materials, methods, and visible explanations.
Treat diversity and homogeneity as active conditions and validate that tasks, materials, interviews, and procedures have comparable meaning across cultures before comparing outcomes.
